speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) moved :

speechtext: I would remind the right hon. gentleman that last Monday he promised that an opportunity would be given to bring up the Fruit Marks Act.
I have not forgotten that promise, and should this motion carry I shall ask the House on Monday to take up the two Bills relating to this subject.

This motion takes away our right to make any private motions whatever, such as motions for returns. Is that necessary ? For instance yesterday a question was put by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) asking how many members or ex-members of the House of Commons have been appointed to offices of emolument under the Crown since the 13th July, 1896, and also how many members or ex-members of the Senate, and he was directed to move for a return. But should this motion carry, it will be impossible for him to do so. There seems to be a remarkable discrimination made between questions put on this side of the House and

those put on the other side. I called attention to this early in the session, and was told by the hon. Minister of Customs that no such discrimination was intended. But let me point to two instances of such discrimination during the session. in the 'Hansard' of March 20th, the hon. gentleman will find a long return given by the Minister of Customs in answer to a question put by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes)-a return which takes up the greater part of the page. 1 called attention to this and was assured by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs that no discrimination was intended. No doubt the question was asked by the hon. member for West Huron, at the request of the hon. Minister of Customs, and with this I am not finding fault, but what I do object to is that we should find in ' Hansard ' an answer to such a question and that hon. gentlemen on this side should hare to move for returns which would not be any more voluminous than the one given in the answer to which I have referred. Another extreme instance is to be found on the 30th of April in ' Hansard.' A certain question was put by the hon. the member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott), at the request, no doubt, of the hon. Postmaster General, and nearly two columns of ' Hansard ' are taken up, without the slightest demur, giving long statistics with regard to three different subjects. Yet when my hon. friend from Marquette asks a question, the answer to which would not take up nearly as much space, my right hon. friend tells him to move for a return. I do not want to unduly complain, but I think that my right hon. friend should make an effort to have the one rule applied to both sides, and I am sure that if that were done, we would not find the condition of affairs to which I have just drawn attention. My right lion, friend must admit that the answer to the question of my hon. friend for Marquette could not possibly involve anything like the lengthy details given in answer to the question of the hon. member for West Assiniboia, but even if it should take a half a column or two columns of ' Hansard, what difference is there ? The minister of the Crown has to bring down the information, and the only difference between bringing it down in reply to a question and bringing it down in reply to a motion, is that in the one case he reads it, and in the other he lays it on the Table. It does not seem to me that so many cases should arise in which so many gentlemen on this side are asked to-obtain information by way of motion. A very inconsiderable portion of some of the business of the House at least has been concluded up to the present, and it is quite possible that we may require information which will be obtainable only by an address or Order of the House, and it seems to me that the right hon. gentleman ought to reserve some opportunity at least to hon. gentlemen on this side for obtaining information which they can only obtain by way of motion. I do not think therefore that my right hon. friend should press the motion in its present form.
The PItIME MINISTER. I must say to my hon. friend that if there lias been any discrimination, I was not aware of it. I would be the last man to try to take an ad-advantage over the other side. It may be, however, that sometimes an answer may more readily give the information than a return in reply to a motion, but there are other eases in which the form of a motion may be more suitable. For instance, with regard to the question of the hon. member for Marquette, I have no objection to give the information desired, but I wish to introduce an amendment and bring down some further information so as to avoid discrimination. Perhaps as the question will involve discrimination, a motion to which I would add an amendment would put all parties on an equality.
That can be accomplished by having a question put on that side.

It would be as well accomplished by having my hon. friend from Marquette move a motion and then moving an amendment to that motion, so that the motion and the amendment would go together. We have come to the time of the session when such a motion is usually moved, and I am only following ihe usual practice. When we have reached a certain period of the session the government takes possession of all the days in order to facilitate, or rather to accelerate, the business of the House. This year, I think, there ought to be no objection at all by my hon. friend to this motion, for, I have only to recall to his mind that, at least of 'ate, on days reserved for private members business, the paper has been gone over, we have been able to finish all the business standing in the nature of private members that was ready to be dealt with and to reach the business of the government. I have no objection that on Mondays, even though this motion is carried, the motions which are not debatable should be called and passed without any objection. Also, we can take up the Bill of my hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Smith) and the Bill of my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson). I think that ought to satisfy my hon. friend.

I would call the attention of the right hon. the First Minister (Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to the fact that I also have a Bill before the House, a very important measure, Bill (No. 20). This has been kept back largely at the request of the government, that they might have an opportunity to consider it. If all the Mondays are now taken by the government, there will be no opportunity to consider this Bill. The Bill has been referred to a special committee. I would

ask the Prime Minister if lie would not allow that also to be taken up.

It is not on the Order Paper. It will be called later on when the committee reports.
Hon. JOHN HAGGAItT (South Lanark). I would draw the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister to the fact that, no matter what the period of the session, this motion was seldom made until the main estimates were all passed. At present the estimates of a good many of the departments have not been even touched. Information may be wanted by members of the opposition to enable them intelligently to prepare for the discussion of the estimates. For instance, three or four points concerning which I have notices on the paper came up in the debate yesterday. I was without accurate information on the subject and could only speak on the facts that I gathered, outside. Opportunity should be left the private members of the House to move motions to get the information necessary for the discussion of the estimates.

With the permission of the House, I would say that I do not agree with the statements of my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) that this motion is generally made only after the main estimates have gone through. It is not only proper, but it is the invariable rule, that all information necessary to the discussion of the estimates should be given, even if not moved for. If it is not furnished, the opposition have a very easy way of enforcing it, and I do not know but that they have availed themselves of that power on occasion even during the present session. With reference to motions of which notice has been given, they will be called up by consent. But even if the motions referred to by my hon. friend are not called up, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) lias promised that the information shall be brought down before his estimates are completed. There will be no trouble on that score. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) shall have the information which lie requires.

Well, we ask for information when the estimates are under discussion and yet it is almost impossible to get it. The minister may promise it, but he may forget, or for some other reason it is not furnished anyway. There is nothing left for us of the opposition but to do as the right hon. gentleman (Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) suggests, and declare that the item shall not pass until the information has been given.

I would suggest one thing, if Monday is the only day we are to have. I notice that when these unopposed motions are called, some member of the government is apt to call * stand,' for some reason best known to the
government themselves. The effect is to prevent the putting of the motion. They could do so with a motion of any kind, and so no opportunity would be afforded to the member who has given notice of a motion to have it passed by the House.

I will tell my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) why the government call ' stand.' W'hen a motion is called and the member in whose name it appears is not present, if nothing were said, the order would be dropped Many debatable questions have been called up in this way. and the hon. member who has given notice not being present, I have called ' stand ' so that the notice might remain on the Order Paper. But on Monday all the motions will be called and those which are not debatable can be passed. For instance, the motion of my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) which stands on the Order Paper is a debatable question and would not be called. But all motions moved for the production of papers will be allowed without any objection.
Motion agreed to.

With the unanimous consent of the House, I would move for :

The interim report of the commissioners appointed to investigate the accident on the Intercolonial Railway near Windsor Junction at 23 o'clock. April 11, 1903.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
House again in committee on Bill (No. 21) to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways.-The Minister of Railways and Canals.
On section 3, subsection 1,

I stated to the committee the other evening that I would consider the suggestions which had been made to include the express companies within the scope of this Act and to place them under the jurisdiction of the railway 117
commission. I have given that subject consideration. and I am not able to see that it will be of any advantage to the Act; on the contrary, I think it would impair its value if we were to make the change which is proposed. I am of opinion that it would be necessary, in order to cover the ground fully and to make the legislation effective, to bring in a separate Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: Does the minister consider that the Bill gives any control at all over the rates charged by express companies ?
The Bill gives absolute control over the rates wfiicli are charged in respect of all merchandise carried over railways, where railway carriage is concerned. There can be no question about that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do I understand that the commission will have control over the whole route covered by express companies in carrying merchandise that is carried on a railway, or only over that portion of a route over which the railroad charges express companies for hauling their goods ?

All charges which are incidental to the carriage of goods over a railway and which would be made in respect of railway carriage, are subject to the control of this tribunal. What is not subject to their control, and what I think cannot be properly made subject to their control, unless we have a separate Act, are the charges which the express companies would make beyond the railway charges. I stated that the other day. I do not think such charges would come within the jurisdiction of the railway commission under this Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would not the result be that wherever the express charge includes anything beyond or in addition to the charge of carriage on the railways, it will not come under the control of this commission ? Because I do not see how you can divide it up. Suppose you have an express charge covering transmission by a certain railway and covering further a certain distance by coach or by boat, there will be only one charge for the entire distance made by the express company. How can you determine what is the proportion of railway charge and what is the proportion of coach charge ?

I do not think that could be very well worked out so as to exercise control over a portion of the charge with respect to another carriage. To do that I think would require a special Act which, to be comprehensive, would have to take control of the rates and charges of express companies in respect to any portion of the route over which it carries goods. I am not dis-



posed to do that in this Bill, I cannot do it comprehensively in this Bill without encumbering the Bill. At another session perhaps the subject can be taken up.
Mr. BOItDEX (Halifax). The hon. gentleman suggests that this additional legislation called for is impracticable. But was there not some such legislation introduced by way of amendment to the Railway Act in 1900, on account of a difficulty which had arisen between the Yarmouth Steamship Company and the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company ? It seems to me that what the hon. gentleman has just stated was attempted by legislation of that kind ; whether it was actually carried out, I do not know.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not think so, I think that dealt exclusively with the rates charged in respect of what was railroad rates in the ordinary sense on goods carried from one point to another, a part of the distance being covered by water carriage. The steamship company had received freight to be taken to some point on the Dominion Atlantic Railway and to be carried by that railway. Then parliament gave to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council power to control that rate, and provided that there should be a declared rate in respect both of water carriage and rail carriage. But there the railway company was the contracting party, or the party who engaged to receive and carry this freight. Now an express company is not in the same position. An express company contracts with its patron to receive a package of goods, not to carry it all the way by rail necessarily, but to carry it to a certain point, and the company is the party which undertakes the carriage. The company may take a portion of it by steamer, it may take a portion of it by carriage over an ordinary highway, and it may take a portion of it by railway. When it gets upon the railway, then, the charges which are made in respect to the carriage of that merchandise will be subject, as I clearly understand this Bill, to the control of the railway commission, because, the railway cannot by any arrangement or understanding that it may have with an agent, or with some other company, or outside party, permit, or secure to itself, any higher rates to be imposed on such carriage than the law through this commission shall declare.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I recollect the case now to which I referred a few moments ago. The difficulty there was in respect to a railway company which also had a line of steamers which connected with Boston. The Yarmouth Steamship Company was a rival company. The allegation was that the railway company had imposed altogether too high a charge for railway carriage on freight routed to Boston by the Yarmouth Steamship Line and in that way had subjected Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
the Yarmouth Steamship Company to an unjust discrimination. The hon. minister's position, I understand, to be this : The express company is a separate corporation undertaking business by any means within its power, and that business can be accomplished partly by railway, partly by carriage over highway and partly by boat, and therefore it does not come within the scope of this Bill to control the rates beyond those which shall be charged by the railway. Well, that brings us back to the position that practically where the express charge covers conveyance beyond the railway we have no control at all. It does bring us back to that conclusion does it not ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not disputing the hon. gentleman's position; I am just endeavouring to find out where we are.
I think the hon. gentleman is right.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then it is a question of policy whether we should undertake to do more and the hon. gentleman thinks we should not.
Not in this Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS ANP CANALS.

speechtext: When the hon. gentleman says: 'not in this Bill' does he intend to convey any meaning beyond that, that he has in mind the preparation of any other legislation which would control matters of this kind ?

I do not hesitate to say that if any difficulty arises in respect to the control and regulation of the tolls or rates of express companies I would not be unwilling to examine into the subject and see whether legislation might not be proposed in another Bill. I would be disposed in my own mind to favour legislation which would give to the public protection against excessive rates being charged by express companies. That is a fair matter for consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I understand the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to say that express matter carried over a railway would be under the control of this commission as far as the rates go ?
As to the railway carriage.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I presume this Bill is modelled largely upon the legislation in the United States under which the American Railway Commission proceeds ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I notice in some decisions on that question given by the Inter-

State Commerce Commission that tins rule is laid down :
Express business, conducted as a branch of the business of the railroad company, held to be subject to the Act.
Express business, conducted by an independent organization, acquiring transportation rights by contract, held not to be described in the Act with sufficient precision to warrant the commission to taking jurisdiction thereof.
They hold that it would be required to be expressed in the Act in such a way as to bring it under the control of the railway commission.

The whole principle of the Acts which provide for the appointment and jurisdiction of a railway commission in the United States and the whole scope and basis of those acts are entirely different from this Bill. I think there is no similarity at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think they are different so far as they are entitled to exercise control over express companies, charges where carried on a railway whether, carried by an independent express company or carried by an express company which is part of the railway company.
You will find there legislation giving control of charges to the commission as respects merchandise handled by a common carrier. That is not the principle of this Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to be a little clearer in regard to a matter that was under discussion when the committee rose the last evening upon which this Bill was under consideration. When the committee was sitting on that evening upon this clause, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals was kind enough to tell me that if I read clause five of this Bill I would find that it did apply to express companies in regard to a ease that I put to the hon. minister; that is a case where goods are shipped by express over a railway that is not within the jurisdiction of this Bill and not within the scope of section three which is before the committee now. T gave the example of an electric railway which runs through the county of Lincoln, entirely a provincial railway, which does not cross any other railway, which does not come within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada and I pointed out to the hon. minister that these goods shipped by the railway I am speaking of from Beams-ville to Ottawa or, say fruit shipped from Beamsville to Ottawa or Montreal, changed hands at Hamilton, were taken from a railway not within the .scope of this Bill and given over to the Canadian Pacific Railway which is a railway coming within the scope of this Bill. The hon. minister told me that if I read section five carefully again I would find that it covered that question, that sec-117*
tion five showed that goods that won Id be carried by express over these two railways, one not within the scope of this Bill, and one within the scope of this Bill, being handed over from the former to the latter in the middle of the journey, would be covered by this Bill. I want to understand this legislation before I vote for or against it. I may be lacking in ordinary intelligence. The hon. minister seems to think that I should read the Bill over three or four times more before I understand it. I would ask the hon. minister to explain how section five meets a case of that kind. Section five reads as follows :-
All the provisions of this Act relating Ao any subiect or matter within the legislative mithor-ity of the parliament of Canada, and for greater certainty but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, all provisions relating to railway crossings and junctions, highway crossings, through traffic, offences, penalties and statistics, shall apply to all persons, companies and railways, whether otherwise within the legislative authority of parliament or not.
It seems to me that no words in that section can possibly apply to express companies unless they are the words ' through traffic.' I do not think that the hon. minister will say that the words ' railway crossings and junctions, highway crossings, offences, penalties and statistics,' will bring any express company within the operation of this Bill in the way in which it was said this Bill would apply. I would now ask the hon. minister whether he means that the words * through traffic ' do cover express companies in cases of that kind, because, if they do, I suppose it follows that the Bill would cover express companies generally, and there seems to me to be a great deal of misunderstanding and a great deal of misconception between the hon. minister and hon. members of this House as to how far these express companies come within the operation of this section. I think it would be well if the hon. minister would point out how section five covers the carriage of express goods by a railway which does not come within the scope of this Bill and which are handed over to a railway which does come within the scope of this Bill. That cannot be covered by this Act at all. The minister said that if I read section five I would find that it covered this exact case, but it can only cover it if it is included in the words ' through traffic.' Will the minister tell us in plain language if the words ' through traffic ' include express business on railways such as I speak of.

The hon. gentleman referred to merchandise which started on one railway and was taken up by another and carried to its destinatiton. That ds through-traffic, and that is provided for by section 5. It is perfectly clear from that section that when a railway company is constituted by the

legislature of a province it does not become subject to the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada ; whether this is so or not, if that traffic was through-traffic in the way he described it, it would become subject to this Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Shipped by express.

I do not care whether shipped by express or not, so long as it is carried over the two railways as through-traffic. I can understand that a doubt might arise if a person in Sarnia were shipping to Ottawa and he sent his goods to Toronto, took them off1 the train, and some one took hold of themiand reshipped them to Ottawa, thus making two distinct shipments. A doubt would probably arise there as to whether the first railway, not being subject to the jurisdiction of this parliament, would be under the control of this commission. But if there is a through shipping over two different railways, and if there is a rate arranged for at first to carry the goods to their destination, then they would become ' through-traffic,' and as such, whether express or not, they would be subject to the provisions of this Act, in my opinion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is not clear yet to a great many of us whether this commission will have power over the rates charged by express companies. As I understand it, the Act will only protect express companies as against the railway companies. The only control this commission would have over rates would be on the railways, and that is but a small part, scarcely half the charge made by the express companies. The express companies make charges for teaming in cities and towns, for the time of their messengers on the train, and for other services, which make up more than half the charges of the express companies, and, so far as I can see, the control which this commission would have over the rates charged by express companies would be of no use whatever to the shipper. Has the minister taken fully into consideration the points mentioned the other night by the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), who stated that Mr. Staunton, an eminent lawyer who considered this matter carefully, had declared that by the insertion of a very few words the express companies could be brought fully within the scope of this Act ? Why should not the minister put a private individual in the same position as an express company, and have it declared in this law that a private individual can ship his goods upon a railway upon the same terms as an express company can ? If that were embodied in the law, it would meet the complaint of shippers of express goods, and of the fruit-growers in particular, who ship the greater part of their products by express, and who are very much concerned about this mattei1. When the fruit-growers interviewed the minister last

winter they never dreamed for an instant that express companies would not be brought under this Act. I can assure the minister that they have always taken it for granted that the express companies would come under the operations of the Act.

I do not know what these gentlemen may have taken for granted, but I think they will find that this Bill will afford them a great deal of relief if they have any grievances of which they can justly complain. At all events, it makes it possible for an independent body to investigate and determine as to whether or not the charges that are made in respect to the railway carriage of these goods are reasonable charges, and if they are not they can reduce them. I read from ' Hansard ' the question put to me the other night by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). He asked :
Now, the question I want to put to the minister is this :	Suppose some constituent of
mine ships his fruit on that electric railway to be carried to Ottawa. It is to be carried by the Dominion Express Company that starts on the Hamilton, Grimsby and Beamsviile Electric Railway, and is then transferred to the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is a railway within the provisions of this Act ? Now, what does the minister say about that express business ?
That is a question of through-freight beyond any doubt, and I answered the hon. gentleman accordingly. I told him that the law provides for that case just as fully as it provides for any case in which business is being done by express companies, and the fact that the initial road was not under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada did not prevent it being brought under the provisions of this Bill as a carrier of through-traffic by the fifth clause, which says :
5. All the provisions of this Act relating to any subject or matter within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, and for greater certainty hut not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, all provisions relating to railway crossings and junctions, highway crossings, through-traffic, offences, penalties and statistics, shall apply to all persons. companies and railways, whether otherwise within the legislative authority of parliament or not. 51 V., c. 29, s. 4, Am.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
As I understand the minister, all freight carried by express companies on railways Is under the jurisdiction of the cojnmission, As my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) has pointed out, that is of benefit solely to express companies and is of no benefit at all to the private shipper. The charges made to the express companies by the railway can be regulated by the commission. But here is an express company which perhaps receives its Incorporation from the provincial legislature and over which the Dominion government has no control whatever. It makes a contract with an individual to carry goods by express over the railroad at a greater charge than the commission allows the railway company to

make. I do not see how under this Bill we could exercise any control over the express company in a case of that kind. I do not say that it ought to be so ; but the Bill affords no remedy at all to a shipper by an express company, and I do not know whether you could in an Act like this make regulations that would do so. Take the case of freight initiated on a road of a purely provincial character like an electric tramway between St. Catharines and Toronto. This Bill provides that the Dominion parliament shall give the commission power to regulate freight charges ; but in a case of that kind, I do not think such a clause is worth the paper it is written on. What right has the parliament of Canada to take control over a company which receives its entity and corporate power from the local legislature, and say that it shall only charge so much for the carriage of goods ? It has no control or jurisdiction whatever over it. I am perhaps with the minister to this extent, that it is rather a difficult job to embody in a Bill like this provisions giving the commission power to regulate express rates, for a good many reasons. Most of the business done by express companies is done under special contracts and at prices which could not possibly be regulated by a commission. For instance, the express companies carry money for banks from the different agencies to the headquarters or to central points, and they make special arrangements 'with the banks under which they receive for the carriage of that money perhaps ten or twenty times the ordinary rate of freight. That is a perfectly legitimate transaction. The express companies are entitled to a large remuneration for the risk they run. Why should we prevent them making such an arrangement, and attempt to provide in a purely railway Bill, that they shall receive no more than is charged for carrying ordinary freight ? I can see the difficulty of the minister in making these provisions apply to express companies. But he could make them apply very easily by adopting the suggestion of the hon. member for Lincoln, which would remedy the whole grievance ; that is, to provide that a railway which carries freight for an express company shall carry the goods of an individual on the same terms and at the same rates.
I do not think my hon. friend would support a motion of that kind.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not say that I would.

There is another important consideration in support of the argument of the minister and the hon. member for South Lanark. People are not bound to go to the express companies at all. We must not forget that this Is a general Bill for a specific purpose, and a very broad purpose ; it is a Bill for railways alone. We
have other general Acts of various kinds ; and if you want to regulate express companies, you can only deal with them intelligently and effectively by means of a general law with respect to express companies, which are different creatures from railways. I think that is logical. We should be very careful, in passing a general Act of any kind, not to incorporate in it things which have no relation to its object. It would he unfortunate, I think, in the interests of the shipper if express companies could not operate in such a way as the lion., member for South Lanark mentions. I do not know what banks or others similarly situated would do. We are prepared to pay extra rates if we want our goods rushed from one point to another by an express company. We often pay for quick expedition in the carriage of goods, and we are willing to pay. If we are going to regulate express companies, my idea is that we should do so by a general Bill dealing with express companies.

I agree that we are quite willing to pay a higher rate for an extra rate of speed, but the express companies do not give it to us. It is the railway companies that give us the speed, because they carry the goods. I would like to ask if there is any provision in this Bill which entitles shippers to demand from the railways the same rate of speed and the same charge for the carriage of their goods which the railways give to the express companies. If so, that will solve the difficulty. In many cases the shipper could dispense with the extra services for which the express company charges the shipper. For instance, he could transfer his goods to and from the railway in his own wagon, and he could dispense with a messenger accompanying the goods on the railway. I would ask the minister if there is anything in the Bill to enable shippers to get the same treatment from the railways as the express companies.

My hon. friend will hardly expect freight to be carried in the same" way as a parcel of goods is carried by express. Freight and passengers are not carried together, but an express car is attached to a passenger train, and in that way goods are carried at an express rate of speed. There is no provision in the Bill which I think would compel a railway company to carry ordinary express freight, as it is* called, at the same rate of speed as carriages containing express goods are conveyed in passenger trains. There is no provision in the law especially authorizing them and I do not know that there is any provision in this Bill which by implication would authorize it. As at present advised I would not favour the introduction of any such clause. By this Bill we confer upon the commission power to determine what is just, fair and reasonable, and we impose penalties of a serious character on a railway company or its officials or anybody connected with it who

would disregard the orders and regulations of the commission, but we cannot undertake to ramify through all the channels of railway operation and discrimination and provide some superabundant power which will meet every possible contingency that may occur to anybody's mind.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
There is another point. The express companies are responsible and not the railway companies. They have to pay an allowance to each railway company. We give them their charters, believing that they serve a useful purpose, and you need not go to an express company unless you please. They are separate corporations, with special powers and are responsible. I am not satisfied that a railway company can undertake this class of business. They may often refuse it. I remember an instance of a railway company wanting to prevent an express company operating on its line, and it was only under a clause of the Railway Act that the company was compelled to do so. The railway company said :	' We will not take that
business at all,' but they found they had to. If the express companies were taking advantage of the public, that would be another question, but the more I consider the point raised, the more I think that it would be an unfortunate experiment to deal with it in this general Bill.

With regard to the statement that railways cannot do this business, the railways in England are doing it. They carry goods at a rapid rate of speed, and if they do not get their cars in on time, they have to pay a fine. Suppose a shipper had a carload of fruit to ship to Winnipeg. He does not want any messenger to go along with it, but is willing to take the responsibility liimsell'. It goes the same way as ordinary freight, except that it goes in a swifter train. If there is no other way of controlling the express companies, why should not the* shipper, if he signs a contract to take the responsibility, have the same rates as the express company ?
The MINISTER Ob' RAILWAYS AND CANALS. I do not think that the passenger trains on English railways carry express goods. They run special fast trains for what they call express freights, but these trains do not run as fast as our express trains. The conditions are quite different.
Amendment (Mr. Maclean) negatived.

I have asked on one or two occasions on what grounds government railways are excluded from the jurisdiction of this proposed commission, and have not yet been able to obtain an answer. Up to the present moment the only reply I have been able to obtain from the hon. gentleman is that he does not wish it. He has given no reason for his wishes. I wish to point out the relative importance of the govern-

ment railway mileage. Take the hon. gentleman's report, I find that the total num-be* of miles of steam railway in the Dominion is 18,868, and electric railways, 558 miles, making a total of 19,426. The hon. gentleman said the other day that 95 per cent of tlie railways would come under this commission. He may have meant 95 per cent of the companies.

I gave the off-hand opinion that 95 per cent of the provincial roads, incorporated under provincial Acts, and which ordinarily would not come under our jurisdiction, had come under it by virtue of the legislation of this parliament from time to time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not holding the hon. gentleman down to 95 per cent. But in a general way he spoke of bringing 95 per cent under this Bill. As I understand, the Canadian Pacific Railway will not come under it, so far as tlie mileage of its main line between North Bay and Vancouver is concerned.
From Callander to Vancouver.

After looking at the time table, I find that the mileage west of North Bay to Vancouver is about 2,542, and that the government railway mileage is 1,552, making a total of 4,094 miles excluded from the jurisdiction of the commission. That would mean that instead of only 5 per cent being excluded, there would be nearly 22 per cent of the mileage of the railway companies excluded from the jurisdiction of this commission. I think that that is a very serious subject for consideration, and while I admit that the hon. gentleman possibly cannot get over the difficulty with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway, it does not follow that he should not have the 1,500 miles of railway operated by the government brought under this commission. I think there is no line of railway which is so important to have under the jurisdiction of the commission as the railway owned and operated by the government. For, this is really the terminal railway. We are discussing in this House the question of adding to the transportation facilities of this country for the purpose of ensuring that the products of the great west shall be directed through our own territory to the sea. The major portion of that traffic may go over the government railway-that is the pipe through which the most of the grain may go. It is of immense importance to those in the west, and to those in the other provinces as well, that the commissioners who control and regulate rates and various other matters as provided in this Bill, should have jurisdiction with regard to this terminal road, the great government road which leads to the sea. There are 1,552 miles of government railway. I admit that

that includes a couple of hundred miles of the Prince Edward Island Railway. But there are over 1,300 miles of the Intercolonial alone, and it is a very important matter that this control of rates by the commission should not be limited so as to exclude that mileage. We are entitled to have from the government something more than their mere wish on this point. There may be reasons why the commissioners should not be allowed to regulate charges upon the Intercolonial, but I believe that the public and that every member of this House will think just the other way. I think that all the discussion we have had in this House, even the elaborate speech with which the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) favoured the House yesterday with regard to his own operations, shows if it shows anything, it is of immense importance to this country that somebody outside of the mere political head of the department should have an opportunity of knowing what is going on in connection with that railway. We are told by the hon. minister that a great discrepancy exists and must exist between the rates charged on the government railway and those charged on other railways. Surely this strikes at the very root of the appointment of this commission. Rates should be fairly regulated, and a shipper should know what rate he is to be charged, not only for a portion of the haul, but for all of it. I persist in the request I have made, and, as I have not had an answer, I move that section 3 be amended by striking out the words ' other than government railways.'

I should have answered, or at least made an effort to answer, the question which the hon. member (Mr. Barker) put to me the day before yesterday, but that we came to a conclusion about the business of the House very shortly after he had spoken, and before I had an opportunity to respond to his appeal. I recall very well the line of argument he addressed to this committee-practically the same as he used to-day-in which he suggested that there was apparently only one reason, or that he had concluded there was only one reason, why this clause should stand ns it does in the Bill, and that was that the Minister of Railways and Canals did not want to hand over the management and operation of the Intercolonial road to the commission, but wanted to continue to be in charge of it himself if he remained in the department. I can only presume that the hon. gentleman speaks under a misapprehension as to the intended scope and purpose of the commission. This commission is not to engage in the management of railways at all; it is a commission constituted to keep the railway companies in check, rt seems to me that upon the very surface a good and sufficient reason is to be found why this Rill should not include the government railway. I do not specially, or even largely,
rely upon the fact that in constituting the Railway Committee of the Privy Council it was thought well not to give that body the same measure of jurisdiction and control over the Intercolonial that was given it over other railways. But it does occur to me that there are the strongest possible reasons why control over the Intercolonial might have been given to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council as constituted, and yet the strongest possible reasons why that control should not be given to this commission as it is to be constituted. If the government owned all the railways operating in the country you would never have heard any appeal or demand for the appointment of a commission. Why ? Because the grievances of which the people complain would never have existed. And, if .they did exist the people would have in their own hands a very ready and very efficient means of remedying their grievances. They would bold tlie government of the day responsible for the perpetuation of such wrongs as those of which many people in Canada complain to-day with respect to the operation of other railways. It is not for the purpose of preventing the Intercolonial Railway from imposing excessive rates upon the people of this country that the railway commission proposed to be created, it is not for the purpose of compelling the Intercolonial Railway to obey this or that law or this or that regulation that the cry has arisen for the creation of a railway commission :	it
is because the other railways of the eoun-try have apparently been so conducting themselves, or, at all events, in the course of their operation, have created such a sentiment in the public mind, that some control of this kind is necessary to be exercised as regards those railways. Now. it is always enough in legislating to remedy the grievances which you know or believe to exist. There is never any advantage in undertaking to remedy conditions which you think may in the future become grievances, but which have not become grievances and are not crying for remedy. The fact that the gov-vernment of the country owns and operates the Intercolonial and is answerable to public opinion for its action and conduct for such administration, is the best reason in the world why you do not require to set up a tribunal outside of parliament for that purpose. It would strike almost any person at first blush. I think, that it would be r. great mistake to confer upon any body of men. I do not care who they might be. control, beyond the reach of parliament or the government. of the management of any public institution and particularly the managment of a railway. You cannot reach them as you can reach the government. They would not be as responsible as to time, and would not be as ready to answer to any demand of public opinion upon them. They might possibly even do something more. Give to this railway commission the powers to fix and determine what the rates are, and they

would have it in their power to compel the people who are doing business over the Intercolonial to pay higher rates than they are paying to-day. I do not see how they could avoid it. They have the power to make uniformity of rates. Here are the standards, they cannot regulate in any way. Here is a standard tariff, here is a special tariff and here is a competitive tariff. They have got to be governed exactly under the same conditions. If you put all railways under the jurisdiction of this commission there is no discretion on their part to except any cne from the operation of the law. I do not think the people of this country are prepared to hand over the power which they now possess through parliament, to any tribunal to interfere with the rates which are charged upon government railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand that the function of that commission would be to fix what would be a just tariff. Therefore, if they fix a just tariff on other railways, why should the hon. gentleman except any railway from coming under a just tariff ?

It is a question of public policy whether or not this parliament is prepared at this moment to make the change proposed. Are there any reasons why the condition of things which has existed ever since we have been a Dominion, when the different provinces agreed to enter into this union, should now be rescinded and that arrangement relating to the Intercolonial be dissolved ? Hon. gentlemen have got to think these things out in their minds a little better before they plunge into amendments of laws which have been on the statute-book ever since this Dominion has been in existence. They must stop and think where they are landing. I do not think the members of this House are prepared, from a national point of view, to make that change. The people of Ontario who do business over the Intercolonial, who sell their goods, manufactured and imported, in the maritime provinces, who do nine-tenths of the wholesale business which is done in the maritime provinces, I do not think they are prepared to say that any advantage will accrue to them by making the rates on the Intercolonial uniform with the rates on all the other roads. I cannot shut my eyes to the fact that the result would be anything but disastrous.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The commission would not have power to raise the rates, if they are now sufficiently low on the Intercolonial, even though they had power to raise them.

If the hon. gentleman will read the Bill, he will find that the commission has not only power to do this, but it is their duty to make such rates in respect of all traffic over any and all railroads as it thinks are just and reasonable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That only applies under the Bill to maximum rates, and the railroad cannot charge less.
Not at all ; there is no maximum business about it. The hon. gentleman has not read the Bill. He will not find the words ' maximum rates ' in the Bill as applied to any measure or scale of tariff.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Am I to understand that the rates charged on the Intercolonial now are less than those charged on other railways in Canada ?

I am quite sure that they are less than are charged on the two great railways of this country, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and always have been. The tariffs are divided into three classes. There is the standard freight tariff, the special freight tariff and the competitive tariff, provided for by section 260 :
The standard freight tariff or tariffs where the company is allowed by the board more than one standard freight tariff, shall specify the maximum mileage tolls to be charged for each class of the freight classification for all distances covered by the company's railway. Such distances may be expressed in blocks or groups, and such blocks or groups may include proportionately greater distances for the longer than for the shorter hauls.
The special tariffs shall specify the toll or tolls lower than in the standard freight tariff to be charged by the company for any particular commodity or commodities, or for each or any class or classes of the freight classification, or to or from a certain point or points on the railway, greater tolls not being charged therein for a shorter than a longer distance, the shorter being included in the longer.
The competitive tariffs shall specify the toll or tolls lower than in the standard freight tariff to be charged by the company for any class or classes of the freight elassificaion, or for an;/ commodity or commodities.
Now, the standard freight tariff is settled in one of two ways. The company may make out its tariff and submit it, and if it is approved, then it becomes the standard freight tariff ; if it is not approved, the board may make out specifically such tariff as they please, and which should be designated as the standard freight tariff.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The argument I was making is this, that the commission seemed to fix the maximum tolls, and it was left to the company to charge any tolls under that. The hon. gentleman stated there was no maximum price fixed at all by the commission.

The explanation of tlie minister, if it can lie called one, has not warranted me in coming to tlie conclusion that the amendment of my hon. friend from Hamilton is wrong, and lias not convinced me that I was wrong in seconding bis amendment, and unless I have better evi-

deuce than I hare now to show why these government railways should not come under the control of this commission, I must vote for that amendment. Now, we are all obliged to the minister for giving us the advice he does, but I think charity begins at home. Let the minister himself take some of his own advice and think a little more carefully about these matters which he asks this House to sanction. The arguments made by the members on this side of the House are made in the interests of the country, because they understand that people want a railroad commission to be a railroad commission in reality, and to attend to the business that it is proposed to submit to it, not to do a patch here and a patch there, not to attend to one section of the Dominion or to one locality to the exclusion of others, but to attend to freight shipped from any part of the Dominion to any other part. A little while ago the minister told us that it was not right that goods shipped from the Niagara district to Ottawa should be under the control of the commission, whether shipped by express or otherwise, but that it is quite right that the whole .journey should be dealt with as through-traffic. I understand him to say that the words ' through-traffic ' in section five are to apply to that. What is the principle that the hon. gentleman has in his mind in regard to that ? Surely it is that there should be no difference whether many or few railways handle the goods. Surely it is that people shipping goods from one part of Canada to another shall deal with the commission in regard to the whole matter and not in regard to any particular part of it. They are not going to be supposed to have a special rate in regard to one railway that the commission cannot control, and another in regard to another railway that the commission can control. If there is any merit at all in the hon. gentleman's Rill it is in that sense. To enlarge the illustration that I gave, suppose any one shipped goods from Halifax to Toronto or from Toronto to Halifax or St. John and these goods are going to be carried by the Gi'and Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway part of the way and by the Intercolonial Railway the rest of the way. What harm is there in the Intercolonial Railway being under the same jurisdiction and having the same authority over it as that placed over the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway ? Suppose that the people in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are not satisfied with the rates, and in view of the discussion that took place in this House yesterday, I can well understand that some of them would be dissatisfied, suppose that they think the rates should be adjusted; if there is any merit in tlie commission there is just as much merit in applying its supervision to the rates charged on the Intercolonial Railway as to those charged on any other railway. If
the Intercolonial Railway is to be dealt with as a business proposition why should its business not be properly carried on and why should not this commission have jurisdiction over its rates in the same way as it is proposed that it shall have over the rates of the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway ? We suppose that the Intercolonial Railway is doing a railway business. It seems to me that the hon. minister is afraid that the rates will be increased on the Intercolonial Railway. I do not know that it would do very much harm if they were increased a little. Perhaps they would not be paying out so much on capital account if they were increased. I suppose that the people would be willing to pay reasonable rates. The hon. gentleman evidently believes that the commission would increase them. I am not at all sure that the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is not right in saying that it is the maximum rates that are to be dealt with. Suppose that the rates charged on the eastern portion of the journey on goods shipped from Toronto to Halifax are altogether inadequate, and we say that the commission shall have no power over the Intercolonial Railway but that they may adjust the rates on the Grand Trunk Railway or Canadian Pacific Railway, surely the members of that commission could not exclude from their minds the rates which the Intercolonial are charging. If they had power to enforce any order that the Intercolonial Railway rates were too high or too low if they could apply that order to the other end of the journey and if they could arrive at a reasonable conclusion, they could the more readily satisfy the shippers and purchasers of those goods. The hon. minister says that he does not think we should legislate for grievances that do not exist, but that we should only legislate for those that do exist. Well, if they are the same kind of grievances they are likely to exist and why should grievances that may exist be excluded from the operation of the Bill. The hon. minister surely does not want full power to do what he thinks the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway ought not to do. I do not suppose the hon. minister wants us to understand that he desires power to do that. If these grievances exist on the large trunk lines, on the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway, and if the Intercolonial Railway is going to spread out (and we hear talk about extending it), is there auy harm in asking that the rates on the Intercolonial Railway shall be controlled in the same way as they are to he controlled on the Canadian Pacific Railway and Grand Trunk Railway ? Are not the same grievances likely to exist on the Intercolonial Railway ? They may not have arisen at present. They may be only about to arise. The hon. minister, for all I know, may expect them to arise next year. If they do arise they will need to be dealt with

by tills commission, ancl there is no harm in the commission having control over the rates on the Intercolonial Railway. In regard to the handing over the power that the hon. minister speaks of, I do not see how that remark applies to the case at all. I do not understand that this commission is to manage the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not think the hon. minister means us to take him seriously when he says that by giving the commission control of the rates on the Intercolonial Railway we would be giving the commission power over the management of the Intercolonial Railway. That is practically what he says. I think there is nothing that will so much cause hon. members on this side of the House to think that the motion of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is right as the weak defence that has been put up by the hon. minister as to why it should not prevail. Upon consideration of all that the hon. minister has said I am firmly of the opinion that the Intercolonial Railway ought to be governed by this commission the same as other railways are, and I shall have to vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Hamilton.

I noticed a few days ago that when the government announced that the canals should be made free that everybody could carry anything he wanted through them without paying a cent, there was not a word from the hon. members on the other side of the House.
What has that to do With it ?

We have spent as much money on the canals as we have spent on the Intercolonial Railway, and everybody can carry everything free through them. We, in the lower provinces, when we travel or when we ship goods, have to pay for doing so.
What has that to do with the Intercolonial Railway ?
It is now admitted, that, if, under the Bill, we applied the commission to the Intercolonial Railway it would be treated like any other railway.
Certainly, why not ?

The Intercolonial Railway was built for the purpose of securing to this Dominion the lower provinces, and it is as much a part of our constitution as if it we re written in. We know that the maritime provinces would not have entered into confederation if the promise to maintain the Intercolonial Railway as a government railway had not been given and carried out. It is as much a part of the constitution as if it were a section of the British North America Act.

That did not imply that
the goods were to be carried for less than
the service was worth.

It implied that the government must always be in charge whether it be Liberal or Conservative, that it must always be a government road because it was built for the purpose I have named. That condition must always be carried out so that our interests shall be protected in accordance with the promise given. We do not desire that goods shall be carried free, although you have your canals absolutely free.
I always thought the building of the Intercolonial Railway was to unite the lower provinces.

It was the condition under which we came in. It was not to unite the provinces. The lower provinces would never have entered confederation had not the Intercolonial Railway been built. We saw the difficulties that would occur, we saw that on everything that we brought from the upper pro1vinces we would have to pay a large price, we saw that the tariff, small as it was then, would be increased and that this new country would be able to build up a large trade in the lower provinces.
Was it not for the same reason that we asked to have the tolls taken off canals-so as to permit of the carrying of goods at a cheaper rate ?
The rates still remain on the Intercolonial Railway. You must take things as they are.
I would like to ask the hon. member (Mr. Fraser) if he is afraid that this commission will do wrong with the Intercolonial Railway ?
No, but if they are honest men they will raise the rates on the Intercolonial Railway.
What does that mean ?
I have no doubt that it will be found that the abolition of tolls upon canals is going to be a good thing in the interests of the trade.

I would like to ask the hon. member (Mr. Fraser) a question. Does he not know that one of the chief objects in making the canals free is to give the maritime provinces the advantage of cheaper goods from the western provinces ?

That is very kind indeed. That is a kindness that we accept with the greatest satisfaction possible. But, coal is not sent through the canals and we do not receive anything in the lower provinces through the canals. Everything we get in the upper provinces comes by the railways, Intercolonial Railway included. What comes through the canals is what goes to foreign parts.
No.
Excuse me, I would like to know wliat we get in the lower provinces that comes through the canals.
Flour.
Excuse me, flour does not come through the canals.
Flour will go.
You are always speculating as to the future. I am talking of present conditions.
Flour is going.
Does not the wheat you get go through the Welland canal.

We don't use any wheat to talk of. You grow the wheat and you grind it and yon grind us by compelling us to pay a duty on it if we buy it any where else. We have no mills down there except a small one in New Glasgow, and I don't know whether it is going or not.
There are some mills grinding native wheat.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We have the ordinary, mills grinding native wheat, but we get no wheat from the upper provinces and consequently the abolition of canal tolls does not benefit us one cent. If you put the Intercolonial Railway under the commission then if they are honest men they will deal with the Intercolonial Railway exactly as with other roads.
Hear, hear.
Would this commission not do a good service to the people of the eastern provinces by preventing discrimination between these people on the part of those who manage the railway?
There never is discrimination.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I speak in the presence of Conservative members from the lower provinces and I say that the railway rates are largely in the interest of Conservatives, because they are the large producers. If the Nova Scotia Steel Company or any 6ther company wants a special rate because they ship in large quantities perhaps it is given to them, but so far as the ordinary business man in the lower provinces is concerned whether they be Liberal or Conservative they are all treated alike, lion, gentlemen opposite want the Intercolonial Railway put under control of the commission, and if the commissioners were honest men they would treat the Intercolonial Railway exactly as they would other railroads, and then we would have the magnificent spectacle of Ontario men getting the benefit of the $80,000,000 we spent on the canals and we would have no benefits from the Intercolonial Railway'. They would have free canal tolls and we would have high railway rates. Is that
broad statesmanship. The condition under which the lower provinces entered into confederation, was that the Intercolonial Railway would be built to cement the provinces together, to give us an opportunity of' consuming western products and to give you an opportunity of consuming our products, but you take very little of the things we produce. It may be a speculation to say' that our coal comes up here, but I notice that some hon. gentlemen opposite, not all, are clamoring that even the duty be taken off coal so that they can get It from the United States when the freights would perhaps be one-third of those on Nova Scotia coal. I care not whether the government of Canada is Liberal or Conservative, I want that government to hold the Intercolonial Railway, to judge what the rates on the Intercolonial Railway shall be, and thus carry out the cementing process that was understood when we entered into confederation.

I have always thought, Mr. Chairman, that it would be in the] best interests of the section of the country I represent that the Intercolonial Railway should come under the control of this railway commission. Ever since the Intercolonial Railway has been in existence it has been operated in direct antagonism to the best interest of the western part of the province of New Brunswick, because the rates on that road have been so low that the products of the upper provinces are carried to the cities of St. John and Halifax for less than we have to pay to carry freight from the county of Carleton and the river counties into these cities. The western produce is thus enabled to come in to competition with the produce that we raise in our section of country. I have thought for a long time that something ought to be done to regulate that. Many years ago I brought this matter to the attention of the late hon. Mr. Rope, then Minister of Railways and Canals, but nothing has ever been done to relieve the situation so far as we are concerned. I believe that it is just and fair that the Intercolonial Railway should come under this commission and that if they are good honest commissioners who will regulate the rates on that road, we will get justice for our section of the country'.

I never understood that it was part of the terms of confederation that we should build a railway to carry freight for less than the cost of handling it. I do not think that you will find in the British North America Act or in the debates on confederation anything that will justify that contention. The argument of the member for Guysborough in favour of that proposition is decidedly unique.
It has often been advanced in this House.

I have heard it repeatedly stated in this House by members from the
3735 .

maritime provinces that they were charged as high freight rates oil the Intercolonial Railway as on other railways in Canada and that they got no advantage. But the member for Guysborough seems to have the idea that the removal of tolls on the canals is for the benefit of the upper province people and that forsooth because of this, the Intercolonial Railway should carry freight below cost for the people of the maritime provinces.
What I said was that the condition that has existed on the Intercolonial Railway since confederation should be maintained.

The conditions on which the maritime provinces entered into confederation has been kept to the letter, but it never was part of the compact that freight on the Intercolonial Railway should be carried below cost, or that the' rates should be so low as not to afford a reasonable profit. Let me tell my hon. friend that the reason why the tolls were taken off the canals was to enable the freight of the west to be carried down to the maritime provinces instead of having it sidetracked off to New York and Boston and other American ports. It was for that purpose and that purpose alone that the canal tolls were removed. The member for Guysborough says that one of the aims should be to carry the coal of the maritime provinces into Ontario.
I did not say what one of .the aims should be. I said it could not be done, and the fact that they were asking to take off the duty on coal in Ontario indicated that it could not be done.
I would remind the hon. gentleman that it not only has been done, but it can be done, and that Nova Scotia coal has been carried as far west as Belleville.
% Then there is no need of taking off the duty.

I want to tell the hon. gentleman that the principle has always been enunciated and supported by the Conservative party that the duty should be kept even on coal, because that was part of the national policy. It is not the Conservatives who are in favour of taking off the coal duty. If the contention was that that duty should be taken off, that was put forward by his own friends in the upper provinces, and not by the Conservative party as a party. As to whether or not the Intercolonial Railway should come under this commission, I have always held that if the commission is expected to do what is right and fair-and we assume that they will be men of intelligence and honest intention-then I cannot understand why there should be any valid objection to the Intercolonial Railway coming under that commission any more Mr. SPROULE.
than any other railway in Canada. If it were expected that they would not do what is right aud fair, I could understand it : but it is expected that they will do what is right and fair-not that they will compel any railway to carry freight at lower charges than will pay, but that they will not allow any unfair discrimination in regard to the short haul and the long haul or between one shipper and another.

Last night the lion. Minister of Railway's explained to the hon. member for Pictou that the rates on the Intercolonial Railway were exactly the same now as they were when the men now in opposition were in power. There was then no word about the rales being too low. But I want to impress on the public outside of this House that the disposition of the opposition, as expressed by the bon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) last night, was to increase the rates [DOT] on the Intercolonial Railway for both freight and passengers. There is another view of tills subject that lias been overlooked altogether, that is, that the carriage over the Intercolonial Railway is not for the benefit of the maritime provinces alone. Hon. members must not forget that the people of the west get the advantage of these low rates in shipping goods to and from the West Indies aud Great Britain in the winter season. I think it would be just as well to leave the management of the Intercolonial Railway in the hands of the hon. Minister of Railways, who has done so well with it during his term. I am sure the hon. member for West Toronto would find the hon. member for Pictou in opposition to his suggestion to increase the rates.
And the leader of the opposition.	[DOT]
The leader of the opposition has been very silent on this subject, because he is not in accord with his own supporters when they advocate an' increase of the rates on the Intercolonial Railway.
I may say that I tever mad<( the statement that the rates on the Intercolonial Railway were too low or too high.
I did not at all attribute anything to the hon. gentleman.

The contention on this side of the House has been that the fact that the Intercolonial Railway is not a paying concern, is due to improper management, not to too low freight rates. We have never, as a party, dealt with the question whether the rates were too liigli or too low. Personally I have never said that they were too low.
Then you cannot vote for this amendment, which says they ought to be raised.
Tlie resolution is tlmt the Intercolonial Railway be included in this commission. It does not say a word about the rates, whether they are too high or too low.

I would like to aslc the hou. minister, if this commission had control over the rates of the Intercolonial Railway, and it found those rates too low, would it have power under this Act to increase them ?
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS ANI) CANALS. There is no doubt about that. I have not any hesitation at all in expressing my opinion. I read the sections which show that the railway commission has absolute power to determine when the rates are just and reasonable, and to impose those rates ; and after it fixes a tariff, until it changes that tariff, you cannot make your rate any more or any less. That is the rate you have to pay.
That is to say, the commission would have power to increase the rates if they found them too low ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It seems to me thatj hon. members from the maritime provinces are unduly excited over this question of rates. I understand that one of the great objects of this railway commission is to secure for the public a general reduction in rates. The contention is that our railways on the whole are charging too much, and our express companies also. In the face of that, why will hon. members from the maritime provinces suppose for one moment that the commission would act directly in opposition to the great purpose for which the commission is being inaugurated ? To my mind, the maritime provinces will be protected under this commission, if the general policy of the commission is what I have stated, and I believe it is. It would seem to me that to make the system uniform all over the country, the Intercolonial Railway should be brought within the scope of this commission, and I, for one, fail to see any cause for alarm on the part of the members from the maritime provinces. While their rights on the Intercolonial Railway will be preserved, I think they will be aided by this commission in securing low rates over other railways from the west.
I do not apprehend for one moment that there will be any interference with the special privileges which the maritime provinces now enjoy.
Mi-. CLANCY. I think if there was any doubt in the minds of the members of this House as to the necessity of having the Intercolonial Railway placed under the jurisdiction of this commission, that doubt has been dispelled by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser). My hon. friend
t has told us that the express terms upon ) which the maritime provinces came into 1 confederation were, first, that there should i be an Intercolonial Railway built

which is admitted-and second, that they should be exempted from paying the same rates ; of freight as are paid by the balance of the people of Canada. That is specifically neither more or less than what , the hon. gentleman has told us. Well, ' I am not prepared to believe that any Minister of Railways will lay down i a rule of that kind. As an illustration of his argument, our genial friend from . Guysborough pointed out that if the Inter, colonial Railway came under the jurisdiction . of this railway commission, the Nova i Scotia Company would be in a worse posi-. tion than it now occupies^
; Mr. FRASER. I said there might be 1 special rates, and I instanced the Nova Scotia Steel Company as large shippers who would be entitled, on that account, to special rates.
Either they are entitled to special rates or they are not.
Like all other large shippers on any railway.

Let me suppose that there will be, as we all hope there will, an institution of the same magnitude at Sault Ste. Marie, which will have to compete at a point half way with the Nova Scotia Steel Company, will the hon. gentleman argue that the latter company would be entitled to the advantage of exceptional rates over the Intercolonial Railway to that competitive point which the other industry could not obtain over the other railways that come under the commission ? Yet that would be the logical outcome of the hon. gentleman's argument. The hon. gentleman also pleads that the tolls are being reduced or entirely wiped out on the canals without protest from anybody. But it seems to me that the amount of these tolls is so insignificant as not to be worth considering. By the abolition of canal tolls, the country is losing the large sum of 8315,425 per year, or less than six-tenths of a cent for each person in Canada.
What I wish to impress on the hon. Minister of Railways is that if we are to have a railway commission, it should not be a meaningless one. The object of a railway commission is to correct the inequalities in freight charges and excessive charges where there is no competiton. Does the hon. gentleman propose that this work of the commission shall be confined to those railways in Canada which are not government railways and that, while all other railways may be forced to do what is fair and reasonable, the Intercolonial Railway is to be exempt from any interference ? The people of this country have contributed large sums for the obtaining of railway

facilities. Are we to handicap these railways which have been aided by Dominion, provincial and municipal bonuses ? Should we not give them a living chance as against the Intercolonial Railway or any other railway that may, according to my hon. friend s contention, be run in the interests of any particular section of the country ? Wliat amount of bonuses has been paid ? The Dominion has contributed to railways in Canada at the rate of $9.0S3 per mile. The provincial governments have contributed at the rate of .$1,177 per mile, and the bonuses given by municipalities have amounted to $S92 per mile.
And we paid equally with you.

That does not touch the fringe of the question. What 1 say is that the people of this country have contributed large sums in order to get railway facilities. My hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Hale) has pointed out that even in the maritime provinces, certain sections are put at a disadvantage by*reason of the lower rates charged by the Intercolonial Railway to other competing sections. How can you expect a private enterprise to supply railway facilities in any section of the country, if the people in that section are getting lower rates on the Intercolonial Railway than are charged by any other railway in Canada ? How can yon expect private enterprise to invest in railways, if these railways are to be swamped by the rates charged on the Intercolonial Railway ? It is all very well for the government to tell the people that they are getting lower rates on the government road. That is a mere electioneering dodge, which may be resorted to by whatever government may be in power.
