If yon charge lower rates on the Intercolonial Railway than the goods can be carried for, or than a private enterprise could carry them at with a reasonable profit, you are simply taking money out of the pockets of one section of people for the benefit of another. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways has told us that had he charged the same rates of freight on the Intercolonial Railway as are charged by other railways, and he went further to emphasize the fact by adding that the rates charged by other railways were not, in his opinion, excessive.
I expressed no opinion as to that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
My hon. friend was especially prudent on that occasion. He was careful not to express an opinion, but he must have assumed that they were not excessive, or lie would have expressed an opinion to the contrary. He told us that if he charged on the Intercolonial Railway the same rates as are charged on other railways, there would be $2,000,000 more in the treasury. Well, what is he doing? He is piling up a capital account of immense magnitude. The Mr. CLANCY.
people of this country are paying on that capital account not less than half a million dollars per year for interest. The hon. gentleman boasts of a magnificent surplus of something like $96,000, but he forgot to tell the people that he is taking out of their pockets half a million dollars in interest on the capital added to our public debt for the purpose of producing this surplus. Is that surplus really an economy or is it not a fiction ? It is the purest kind of fiction, a mere juggling of figures, a mere deception on the public, a brazen attempt to make the people believe that they have saved $96,000, whereas in reality they have been bled to the tune of half a million dollars. If we are to have a railway commission, I can see no reason why the Intercolonial Railway should not come under its jurisdiction. It certainly should, if we are to do every section of our people the same justice. Suppose that the dream of the hon. gentleman were to be realized, in which he indulged when out to the Pacific coast last fall. Suppose the hon. gentleman were to do what he is hinting at as possible, and build a transcontinental line at the public cost. That road, being a government road, would not come under the jurisdiction of this commission. So, the hon. gentleman would be able to say to the people :	Being beyond
the control of the commission, I can do as I like with rates, and I will give favourable rates to those sections which support me, and unfavourable rates to others. It is impossible not to see what the effect of such a state of affairs would be. Wo have [DOT]devoted millions to the subsidizing of trunk lines to the Pacific coast, and the government road would have no right to become an unfair competitor with those lines, and to use for the purpose of competition 'ts advantages in the way of freedom from taxes and from the obligation which rests upon railways of earning interest upon the cost of construction. Nothing could be more destructive of our great national outfit, our railway system of which we are so proud. It woiild be contrary to justice, contrary to common sense, contrary to every business principle. There is no reason why there should be a lever in the hands of the government to give favours that cannot be given to the people in common. What do we hear with regard to other classes of trade ? There has been a cry that convict labour should not be allowed to come into competition with the honest wage-earner. I say that is a good contention. To act upon the contrary principle would be use-ing public institutions against private interests ; and I say that it would be wrong to use the Intercolonial Railway or any other road owned by the government to injure private interests. It might yield apparent advantages to a section of the people, but advantages which must be paid for dearly by the people at large. I say again that I know nothing more contrary to rea-

'foil, common sense and business principle, than the suggestion that the Intercolonial Railway should not come under control of this commission.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) has asked a question. But first as to what the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hale) says. 1 can understand him when he says that the produce from the province of Ontario comes through his county, carried on the Intercolonial Railway at cheap rates, and comes in competition with the produce of the farms of Carleton. But the public of the lower provinces know that the county of Carleton canuot supply them with everything they require, and so they want others to come in and supply them. And- even though it be considered small-they are of opinion that it is better that the county of Carleton should suffer to a limited extent rather than that the whole of the lower provinces should suffer. Referring to the lower provinces, 1 desire to say one thing, and in this I speak for Nova Scotia alone. Nova Scotia has given more per head to build railways, either to compete with or to feed the Intercolonial Railway than has been given for railways by the people of any other province in the Dominion. Moreover, Nova Scotia has received less money per head voted by the parliament of Canada for railways than the people of any other province of the Dominion. The return was brought down to this House which proved it. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy), has got away from the fact of the canals. Whatever the rates are on the Intercolonial Railway, at least this year we have a surplus. But we have never had a surplus on the canals. And this year we are adding two or three hundred thousand dollars as a free gift to the people who benefit by those canals, to be added to the deficit. There would be judicious management of the Intercolonial Railway whether the Conservatives or the liberals were in power. And we must not forget the long distance between the lower provinces and Montreal, which is covered by the Intercolonial Railway. Cannot we trust the making of the rates upon this road much better to a government that can consider broad questions of the public interest than to a commission that must rigidly enforce the law, and that must insist upon rates-
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser) permit me ?
Yes.
Is he presuming that the commissioners will be enforcing an unjust law ?

That has nothing to do with it. I say you can trust the government, whatever party that government may represent, to fix the rates in the best interests of the country. There is also the consideration that the Intercolonial Railway was built to bring about confederation, a fact that has been stated in this House a dozen times in my hearing and never contradicted until to-day. Any government will do better in the interest of the whole country than a commission that must simply follow the law, caring nothing for the people. The rates on the Intercolonial Railway have been substantially the same since the road was built-do not hon. gentlemen think that we can reasonably expect that road to carry out the same in the future ? The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) looks at it from the Ontario standpoint, but he forgets to take into consideration the canals which were built largely for the benefit of Ontario, and which never had a surplus and never will.
We on this side have never defended or condemned taking off the canal tolls, or expressed ourselves on that subject. Let the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser) look to his own friends for that.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) does not favour the removal of the canal tolls he has the opportunity to express his opinion, and, as a member of this House, to move that they be not taken oil. The fact that he expresses no opinion and moves no motion on the subject, ranks him with those who are in favour of the change.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fraser) is simply putting up a man of straw and knocking it over.

We have heard now from two prospective ministers, for the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), and the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), if I am to judge, must he in any government formed by the leader of the other side. If these bon. gentlemen had their own way they would increase the rates on the Intercolonial Railway in the lower provinces. If their attitude means anything, it means that. AVe understand it now ; that is the way our Conservative friends would treat the Intercolonial Railway.

The question before the committee is simply this-shall the Intercolonial Railway come under the jurisdiction of this commission or not. As an argument to the contrary, the hon. Minister of Railways states that, being responsible to parliament and to the people in fixing the rates, the people would have better control than if the commission were given jurisdiction over the road. I stated that the commission had nothing to do with fixing the rates on the Intercolonial Railway. They only fix the maximum tariff, and under that maximum the minister could make any charge he liked. The minister contradicted me when I stated that. He asked me if I had read the Act, and stated that the commission had the right to fix the tariff of

tolls and that the government would be obliged to exact those tolls from any one using the Intercolonial Railway. There was no one on this side who said that the tolls charged on the Intercolonial Railway were less than those charged on the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk Railway. It was the hon. Minister of Railways himself, when he was appealing to supporters from the maritime provinces. He turned around to them and said : ' I could have a surplus of $2,000,000 if I were allowed to charge the same rates on the Intercolonial Railway as are charged by the other railways.' I would like the hon. gentleman to point out in what respect the charges on freight traffic or the charges on passenger traffic are less on the Intercolonial Railway than on the Grand Trunk Railway or Canadian Pacific Railway.
Let me mention the passenger freight rate on the Intercolonial. You pay three cents a mile, and if you get a return ticket you get it for one and a half the full rate. Isn't that the same custom on every railroad of the Dominion ? Don't you pay the same when you travel on the Intercolonial as we do here ? There may be a couple of mines from which coal is carried to Halifax, there may be exceptional cases where freight is carried lower on the Intercolonial than elsewhere; coal is carried from particular mines to Halifax or to some favoured lumberman at specially low rates. But the poor farmer, the industrious man, the traveller in every portion of the maritime provinces pays as much for the user of the Intercolonial as we do for the user of onr railways in the western part of Canada. That is why the control of rates on the Intercolonial should come under a commission. As I said last night, the reason of the apparent reduction of rates on the Intercolonial, the reason of the loss in carrying freight, was an effort on the part of the minister to carry freight which would naturally follow other channels, and to divert it in an tin-natural course to St. John or to Halifax. We will have a comparison of the freight rates before the estimates are through, we will have a comparison of the passenger rates, and I venture to say that my statement will be found correct. The hon. gentleman is indulging in parish politics of the lowest kind. He is appealing to his followers on the back benches, saying; Look at the glorious things I have done for you in the management of the Intercolonial ; look at the envy it has excited throughout the Dominion. I am giving you cheaper passenger rates and cheaper freight rates, and these people in Ontario and in the west, if they had the power, would impose upon you rates entirely different. The minister is perfectly correct, and the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) is correct; there has been but little change in the rates on the Intercolonial from its inception, either under the Conservative government or the Liberal government. But the rates are fair,

they ought to pay, and possibly, if through rates were imposed, there might be a greater return to the people. All we ask is a fail-rate for passengers, a fair rate for freight. That fair rate is being imposed upon the people. Under good management and economical management the Intercolonial, instead of being a drag and an imposition on the people, would give us a fair return for the expenditure. We have no wish to impose on the people of the maritime provinces. When w4 talk about the management of the Intercolonial we are not finding fault with the charges that are made on passengers and on freight to people using the road locally ; we are only asking that economical management should be exercised.
But to return to my question. What objection is there to the appointment of a commission whose principal object and work would be to fix and control tbe rates and tolls ? Surely the minister does not think that the rates and tolls fixed by a commission would be less than those that he now charges on the Intercolonial. Then what has he to fear ? There may be arguments advanced on both sides of this question. My hon. friend thinks that under the absolute control ' given to the commission they would have power, not only to control the rates, but the appliances to be used, the speed to be observed in the running, the rolling stock and everything else. Perhaps it would be better. We know the powers of commissions appointed by governments in other countries for the purpose of dealing with railways. It is the commission which steps between the individual and tbe railway company, as a sort of arbitrator, to say what is just and right in reference to the dealings between the general public and the company. My own opinion is that it would be better for the Minister of Railways and Canals to be directly responsible to this House and to the people. I would not like him to have a further opportunity to shield himself behind a commission. If he does wrong, let him come here where he is responsible to this House, and we will talk to him and find out all about it. In a government railway. T think that the controller of it should be directly responsible to tbe people of the country and to parliament, and that there is not much call for the interference of a commission.
We have been told on this side of the House by hon. gentlemen opposite that the Intercolonial is an institution which is run in the intex-ests of the maritime provinces.
Nobody said so.

Well, I have heard some hon. gentleman say that the deficit incuiTed by the Intercolonial in the maritime provinces was paid by the people of Canada generally, and for the express advantage of the people of the maritime pi-ovinces. Now, I think that hon. gentlemen opposite will recollect that a few months ago the board

3 * 4b
of trade of tl)e city of Halifax passed a resolution calling upon tlie government to hand over the Intercolonial to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I do not think that was exactly the tenor of the resolution. The resolution asked the boards of trade throughout Canada to consider that question.

Yes, and I suppose there was never a greater storm raised among the boards of trade throughout Canada than that very resolution of the Halifax board of trade. How did they take it up ? The boards of trade in Moncton, in St. John, in Quebec, in Montreal, and the board of trade of the city of Toronto, which I presume has the confidence of hon. gentlemen opposite, passed strong resolutions condemning the proposition to turn over the Intercolonial to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I presume that the board of trade of the city of Toronto represents fairly well the manufacturers of Canada, the manufacturers of nearly everything in which iron enters, the manufacturers of textiles. It represents the millers of Canada, who send hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of their products to the maritime provinces every year ; and they recognized that the working arrangement between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Intercolonial in the maritime provinces affords them protection against the excessive rates which might otherwise be charged by the Canadian Pacific Railway which runs to the city of St. John. I presume that the board of trade of Toronto did speak with some authority for the great manufacturing classes of Canada when it said that it was thoroughly satisfied with the administration of the Intercolonial. The hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) suggested that the rates might be raised on certain commodities going over the Intercolonial. He intimated that certain privileges were being granted to the lumbermen. I wish to point out that only this year, when the lumbermen of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick approached the Minister of Railways and Canals and asked for certain reductions in the freight on lumber to the seaport, that request was refused, and I think we will all say very rightly refused. If, two years ago, those lumbermen could make money when deals were selling for $9 and $10 a thousand, they must be making more money to-day when they are bringing $13 or $14 a thousand. I would not be opposed to seeing the rates on lumber carried by the Intercolonial raised to a certain extent. The hon. gentleman intimated too that coal was carried at too low a rate. That may be correct, but it is a pretty serious matter for this House to say that the rates on coal should be raised, serious for the consumers of coal in Quebec and Montreal. I recognize that the coal companies of Nova Scotia are charging the consumers of coal too much for their coal, but 118
how are you going to benefit the consumers of coal by raising the price of the carriage of coal to Quebec and the eastern part of Ontario. I think if the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) were again entrusted with the responsibility of being Minister of Railways and Canals he would hesitate, because numbers of his supporters would call upon him to hesitate, before he would raise the rate on the carriage of coal. We in the coal mining districts do not get the benefit of these rates, but the people In the west do.
I failed to hear any one on this side of the House contend that coal was carried too cheaply.

Mr. Chairman. I think the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) Is not doing quite justice to this quesion when he speaks of the origin of this discussion in regard to freight rates on the Intercolonial Railway. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Air. Blair) made this statement in the House when he was presenting the affairs of the Intercolonial Railway to parliament.
That important portion between St. John and Halifax is, I think, paying quite a handsome return over its cost and the expenses of operation.
Now, I suppose this statement is only consistent with fair rates being charged. In so far as I am concerned it was news to me yesterday to hear the announcement of the hon. Alinister of Railways and Canals which I am about to read. I am sure the people of the maritime provinces do not want the Intercolonial Railway conducted on any system which is not fair to the people of the rest of Canada. They do not want the Intercolonial Railway conducted on a principle which would make the people of the rest of Canada pay any portion of the freight charges which should be paid by the people of the maritime provinces. At the same time they do have regard to the fact that the Intercolonial Railway was part of the terms of confederation and there may be circumstances which would justify the reduction of freight rates upon that railway to a point perhaps lower than those charged upon some other railways. These are conditions which should be viewed just as much by commissioners as by the government of the day in the administration of the Intercolonial Railway. They ought to be considered by the commission just to the same extent as they are supposed to be considered by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. Therefore, it seems to me, "that a large part of the discussion in regard to whether the rates should be controlled on the Intercolonial by the commission or by the government is beside the question, because exactly the same consideration should apply to dealing with this matter by the commission as to dealing with it by



the; hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. Now, I think it is most unfortunate that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals should have made the statement which he did make in the House yesterday unless he is absolutely sure that the facts are-as he states them. As I said before, I have no means of knowing whether the facts are as the minister has stated them. I will read to the committee the remarks of the hon. minister which led to this entire discussion and which, I think, placed the people of the maritime provinces in a false position in regard to the people of Canada as a whole. I suppose that the hon. gentleman by stating that the rates on the Intercolonial Railway afford a fair return as between Halifax and St. John, and a certain portion of the maritime provinces has stated that these rates are fair rates. 1 do not know what else the statement means. If they afforded a fair return on a portion of the road in a fairly thickly inhabited district surely they must be regarded as fair rates. Tha hon. gentleman has made that statement, but notwithstanding that, he goes on to say this :
I had a careful -study -made and a careful statement furnished to me by the traffic officers of the Intercolonial Kailway as to the general tariff of tolls -and freight charges which governs on the Intercolonial Railway and those which govern on the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway; and the result of that statement, keeping well on the safe side, is that the rates upon those two railways are from 50 to 100 per cent higher than those upon the Intercolonial Railway. I am not going to suggest that the rates upon either of the two other roads -are higher than they ought to be.
Well, if the rates ou the Intercolonial Railway in Nova Scotia afford a fair return and if these rates to which the hon. gentleman refers in Ontario are from 50 to 100 per cent higher, I think the hon. gentleman ought to be able to form an opinion upon them, although he says he has no opinion whatever. I think it is important that the hon. minister should place upon the Table of the House the information upon which he relied when he made that statement, and which I do not think does justice to the people of the maritime provinces as far as the Intercolonial is concerned. I have a great deal of doubt, with all deference to my hon. friend, as to whether or not his statement as to the rates being 50 to 100 per cent higher will be found to be exactly borne out by the facts. I am not impugning the varacity of my hon. fx-iend, but I must say that I shall have my doubts until the information is placed upon) the Table of the House as to whether or not that statement is correct. I would like to ask the hon. minister whether or not it is a fact that these i-ates have to be submitted to him as Minister of Railways and Canals or to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. Is it not a fact that these rates cannot be raised until he has approved of them ?
Freight rates are subject to approval by the Governor in Council. Until they are approved they are not collectable, or they are not supposed to he collectable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I have not been quite clear this afternoon during the discussion, a<s to whether my estimates were under consideration or whether the Railway Bill was being-dealt with. The debate has passed from one theme to the other, so that it was almost impossible to discriminate as to what was in the minds of the gentlemen who are addressing the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You did the most of that yourself.
Does the committee hear my hon. friend deliberately and coolly state that I occupied the most of the time of the House ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The question was started by the minister's own friends and replied to from this side of the House.
I do not think that I spoke more than once or twice when I was called up by members of the committee.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And then you were worse than the Minister of Agriculture.

I shall be very glad to furnish to the committee the information which has been supplied me in regard to this question of the freight rates upon the Intercolonial Railway. I was, however, amazed to hear the ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Haggart) state that the local rates are the same upon the Intercolonial Railway as they are upon the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway in other parts of Canada. I felt very much like turning the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) over to the tender mercies of the member for Carleton (Mr. Hale) who complained that to his knowledge the Canadian Pacific Railway charges on freight from Woodstock to St. John were so much higher than the Intercolonial charges for the same kind of freight that it was a serious handicap for their business and that the people of the county of Carleton and the river counties were not able to place their goods in St. John in fair competition with the goods carried over the Intercolonial Railway. I leave my hon. friend (Mr. Hale) to deal with the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) and to tell him that he was not really well informed as to what was doing on the Intercolonial Railway when he was head of the department. At my request one of my officers has supplied me with a statement which will show the difference between the rates which are in force on the different railways, and I will furnish that to the committee. I move that the committee rise.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I have not stud-died the Bill perhaps as attentively as I

should, but, is it a part of the scheme of this Bill that railways should be prevented from giving lower rates than those fixed by any one of the tariffs referred to in the Bill.

speechtext: If these proceedings in the case of the municipality of Valleytield were initiated by the commanding 'officer, how comes jt that this correspondence is in the office of the hon. minister? speechtext: By whom ?

speechtext: It would appear from this correspondence that the suit must have been commenced through the Department of Militia here or by others with the commanding officer, because it refers to the fact that there are others connected with Colonel Roy as plaintiffs. On the last page of the file there is a letter from the Justice Department stating that there were no steps taken through that department relative to this suit. May 1 ask the minister if he is aware who Sir. Edgar N. Armstrong is, and whether instructions were given by the Department of Militia and Defence to Mr. Armstrong to commence the action 7 I assume from the record, that Mr. Armstrong is a solicitor in the city of Montreal.

The proceedings seem to be carried on by direct correspondence with the commanding officer, instead of through the Justice Department. It might be open to the department to commence pro-

ceeclings in that way, but I think that an examination of the precedents will show that such proceedings were formerly commenced through the Justice Department. I know that was the course under the former regime, and I think it is the proper one. I notice by the memorandum that the department instructed that proceedings be commenced by the commanding officer. It says : ' Instructions to take legal proceedings were sent to the commanding officer of district No. 5 on the 3rd April, 1901.' That is from the department
The military branch.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Of what ?

Of the Militia Department. It does not seem to me a desirable way of proceeding, to pass over the charge of these matters to the commanding officer, who is in no way interested, as I remarked the other evening, except as a trustee for the department. Can the minister explain why instructions were not sent to the Department of Justice to proceed to collect this money ? There ought to be some explanation, it seems to me, unless the minister considers that he has pursued the proper course. So far as my judgment goes, his course is irregular. We have a Justice Department here at the service of the government, which should take proceedings in the regular way, and the head of that department is responsible to the government, to parliament and to the country. But instead of that, the hon. gentleman seems to have imposed this duty on the commanding officer. Now, I think the constitutional way is to hand it over to the Justice Department. Besides, the Militia Department is not equipped to take these proceedings at all. Surely the hon. gentleman will recognize that parliament must hold the minister responsible, and therefore he should utilize the proper department of the government to institute proceedings of this sort. It seems to me an unusual proceeding.

My hon. friend was here the other evening when these estimates were discussed, and he heard the Minister of Justice state that it was a matter which the law fixed, and that the department here, in the first instance, had nothing to do with it. The law reads as follows :-
When the active militia, or any corps thereof, is so called out in aid of the civil power, the municipality in which their services are required shall pay them, when so employed the rates authorized to be paid for actual service
to officers, men.... And in addition, shall
provide them with proper lodging, and with stabling for their horses ; and the said pay and allowances for subsistence and forage, as also the value of lodging and stabpng, unless furnished in kind by the municipality, may he recovered from it by the officer commanding the corps, in his own name, and, when so recovered, shall be paid over to the persons entitled thereto.
Under that clause the general officer commanding, as my hon. friend will see if he reads the General's letter, instructed the district officer commanding who called out the troops, that it was his duty to act. and the department had nothing to do with it, at that stage at any rate, and have no other obligation in the matter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: My sole object in dwelling upon this matter now is to get the minister to take a stand on what he considers to be the constitutional practice that should be followed under these circumstances. When the municipality does not pay the troops the law explains that the department should pay them-that is what happened here. Now, while the law does say that the commanding officer should, in his own name, take action, the money is not going to the commanding officer, but to the Militia Department. Naturally, as the government have paid the money, they have a right to collect it, and the commanding officer has no business to touch it. My object is to get the minister to say on his responsibility what procedure ought to be taken. I contend that under the proper construction of that law the Justice Department should enforce it and take proceedings to recover. It becomes a legal matter then, and it is for the Justice Department to see that legal proceedings are taken. I want to press this matter in order that the militia officers may understand the construction that is put upon it. I think if the officers understood that they are to take these proceedings at their own risk, on their own responsibility and at their own expense, you would very soon find them declining to act as commanding officers. I expressed myself strongly the other night on the same line, and the conclusion of the discussion was that the minister should bring down the information, as he has done, that we might discuss the question more intelligently. Now, we find that the Militia Department instructed the officers to proceed. I say that is not a proper course to follow, because the money to be recovered belongs to the country. Does the hon. gentleman know of any other similar cases that have occurred under his administration ?
There has been one case in British Columbia.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: How did you proceed then ? Did you pay the troops ?
We paid the troops, and took proceedings to recover in the same way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Was the case sent to the Justice Department to recover the money ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
You directed the
commanding officer there to do it ?
Yes, lie was reminded of liis duty, and he proceeded to collect, and did collect In that case, I think.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Well, I think it is time attention was called to the irregularity of proceeding in that way. I submit that is not what is intended under a fair construction of the law. The statute had to provide for some person to bring the suit. But if the practice the department has been following is according to law, the law ought to be promptly changed, and that is the reason why I am laying stress on this matter. Under the old regime, this course would not have been taken. The law is sufficient in its present form if it was carried out in a constitutional way. If the commanding officer had to pay the men himself it would be a different thing, because then he would be acting for the men. I submit that If the law is to be so construed that this money must be collected by the commanding officer, the law should be amended.

I think the point my hon. friend has taken is well worthy of consideration. I am not a lawyer myself, therefore I am at a disadvantage as compared with him. I assume that the practice followed in this case was the same as the practice followed in preceding cases that have happened. There have not been many, but there have been at least two before this one, one in my time and one before. My deputy minister is a lawyer, and I have a good deal of confidence in him, because he has had a good deal of experience, and I felt quite sure he was pursuing the proper course. I may say at once that I think it will be very proper to submit the question which my hon. friend has raised to the Department of Justice to have our position defined under the statute. I am not able to construe the statute. I have simply stated the construction which was put upon it the night before last by the hon. Minister of Justice within the hearing of my hon. friend. So far as the expense to be incurred by the district officer, or the commanding officer, is concerned, it does not seem to me that there is any question as to that. I do not think there could be any doubt under the statute that where an officer is compelled to do a certain thing it must be understood that the money shall be provided for him, and that he shall not be put to any expense. It does not seem to me that that can admit of argument at'all, no matter what course is pursued. It cannot be presumed for a moment that a person who is compelled to bring this suit shall be expected to do so at his own expense.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I do not think there should be any difficulty whatever in working out the statute in that case. As a matter of fact I think that in practice the pay and allowances for the men are provided

by the government because usually there is some delay before a municipality pays them over. A suit in regard to a similar matter in the province of Nova Scotia went first to the Supreme Court of that province and then to the Supreme Court of Canada. There was no difficulty about it. The department hands over to the men the pay and allowances provided by the statute. Well, then, the department having done that, the commanding officer, not for his own benefit, or on his own account, but on account of the government, calls upon the municipality for the reimbursement of that amount. The commanding officer is merely the trustee for the government, because the government have paid the money and are entitled to recover it in the name of the commanding officer. The practice pursued in the case I refer to is this : The municipality declined, or neglected to pay over the money to the commanding officer, the Department of Militia and Defence simply placed the case in the hands of the Department of Justice and the Department of Justice instructed its agent to take tjfie necessary proceedings for recovery. These proceedings were taken. A question arose as to the sufficiency of the requisition in that case, ns to whether or not the requisition came within the terms of the statute. That case was eventually decided in favour of the Crown and the amount was recovered from the municipality in question. The commanding officer is a mere figure head. He is simply a trustee for the government. If he refuses to take action the government would still have a remedy. That is beyond doubt, and I do not know why there should be any difficulty in a case of this kind more than in any other case, because, the fact that he refuses should not in any way effect the right of the government to recover from the parties who are liable as the law provides. In so far as the hon. Minister of Justice makes any argument to the contrary, I am not clear as to what he means. In so far as he makes an argument to the effect that this is only a matter for the commanding officer, I do not agree with him. There cannot be any question about that. The commanding officer is simply the person in whose name the statute has authorized the suit to be brought. The object is 'very clear. In the first place the liability is created between the municipality and the officers and men who are entitled to their pay and allowances. It would be inconvenient for every one of these men to sue the municipality; therefore. the statute provides that the action shall be taken in the name of the commanding officer. Another provision is necessary. That is that the men shall be paid while the questions arising with the municipality are being determined by the courts. Therefore, the statute provides that the government may advance these moneys, but it also provides that this shall in no way interfere

with the liability of the municipality. Then, it says that the commanding officer shall proceed to sue, and that upon the recovery of the amount he shall pay it over to His Majesty. He is what in law- is called a bare trustee for the Crown, having no personal interest whatever. There should be no difficulty in working out the statute and taking the necessary proceedings to recover the money.

speechtext: I understand that the minister has declined to bring down the special report which has been made by the major general commanding. Would the minister please repeat his reasons, as I will probably have something to say about it later on.

speechtext: I am not speaking of the Defence Committee report.

speechtext: The minister's explanation of what the report is
It; is a defence scheme.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I quite agree that a defence report should not be published because it is a plan by which an enemy could be most successfully met. but I do not understand from the explanation of the minister that the report in question is of such a nature. I thought it was a report on what the major general believed would put the militia of Canada on an efficient Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
footing. In his annual report, the major general says :
With this report I have the honour also to forward another special report to which I have given a great deal of thought, and it contains a broad scheme for the improvement of the militia. If the proposals contained in it are carried out they will in my opinion conduce to the greater efficiency of the militia.
It would not appear from this that there would be anything secret about the report. There may be reasons why the minister would not carry out the recommendations in that report, the expense among other things, but seeing that the major general does not say that it is a confidential report, I do not think the minister should take the responsibility of keeping it from parliament. I have not the honour of knowing Lord Duudonald even by sight, but he is an officer of very high reputation and very great experience, qualities which commend him highly to the people of this country and to the militia force, and consequently his views on what would add to the efficiency of our militia are extremely important to the public, and I have no doubt would be very beneficial if they could be carried into effect.
With all deference to my leader, and with all the confidence that I have in him, I do not think the private examination of that report should be left to his responsibility. I think we are all entitled to get the benefit of it. At this time especially, when the relations of the colonies to the Empire, particularly in regard to defensive measures, are a live question, it would be most opportune to have a scheme devised by a man of the capacity and responsibility of the Major General Commanding, and endorsed by the government. I am one of those who have no desire for what is called militarism in the sense in which that word is generally used. I think we ought to do our share, and we ought not to be afraid to do our full share, of providing for the defence of this country, and if we do that, it may be fairly taken as our quota towards the defence of the empire. That is my idea at the present time of the distance we should go in that direction. I know of nothing that would be more satisfactory to myself, as a representative of the people, and I believe to all other representatives of the people in this House, and to the militia force, a part of which made such a splendid record for themselves in fighting side by side with the force which in case of need would help us to defend this country. I regret that the minister has taken the view he has expressed. I hope I may be able to induce him yet to reconsider his decision. In my opinion he will make a serious mistake if he does not submit the report to the public view. It will be a mistake for him in his position, for his department, and for the government, and a disappointment to the force, if we are not allowed to see that report, prepared by a great and experienced

soldier, one of the finest officers, from liis record, in the British service. Let ns see it and judge for ourselves. I do not think it is at all on the line of the defence report. There were most important and essential reasons why that should be secret, but none of those reasons seem applicable to a report of this sort. While the scheme may be too large and too expensive in many ways, yet 1 think it would be an excellent thing for us to have the views, extravagant or otherwise, contained in this report as to what will be necessary to put our militia into an efficient shape, and as to the proper size of that force. I am more than ever desirous of seeing it for this reason. So far the Major General and the minister have not shown a disposition to expend money extravagantly in the way of training the militia. They are introducing some new features. Probably from what the hon. minister says about the supplementary estimates, and about postponing the discussion until we have them before us-, we may have some statements at that time in regard to those features. But in the meantime I hope he will change his mind and allow this report to be seen and judged by all the people of this country.

I thought it was understood that we were to postpone this discussion ; but I am afraid my hon. friend is rather inclined to anticipate the discussion on the item which I agreed to bring down later on. I thought that was the proper course to pursue, because I hope in the supplementary estimates to have some items on which a discussion of this kind can properly be raised. Of course, my hon. friend has the advantage of me in coming to a judgment of the report he is talking about, because he has never read it, and I have. Let me repeat to him that the report is in my judgment very similar to that of the defence committee which sat here in 1898. That report has been adopted by this government, and approved by the intelligence branch of the War Office, with which we must be in touch in carrying out our defensive schemes in this country.' I do not think it is wise to pursue two lines of a defence scheme at once. I prefer to get rid of one before I begin with another. When the estimate which I have to bring down is brought here, I propose to take the House into my confidence, so far as I can, with reference to the contents of the defensive committee's report of 1898 and the contents of the Major General's report of a recent date.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
What the hon. minister has just stated would rather confirm the widespread rumour that there was a difference of opinion between the General Officer Commanding and the hon. minister respecting this report ; and if we look at the statement in the Militia Report, submitted by '
the General Officer Commanding, we shall see that he finds a good deal of fault with the way in which the militia force of Canada is conducted, for instance, in the matter of equipment. I would like to know how we are going intelligently to discuss the estimates of the Militia Department without being in possession of all the necessary information. I submit that the hon. gentleman should at least give us that portion of the report which it would not injure the militia to make public ; and instead of the minister reserving his general statement until the supplementary estimates are brought down, if that statement had been made when the estimates were first introduced, we would be enlightened as to his policy with respect to the militia of this country. But not knowing what the policy of the hon. gentleman is, I fail to see how we can discuss these estimates as they ought to be discussed.

With reference to defence schemes and confidential documents, the history of European countries shows that these are largely instruments to encourage some confidential clerk to sell them to neighbouring agents. I do not know that there should be any confidential scheme of defence for Canada. The cheapest confidential scheme would be to have all our young fellows trained to be good shots so that they could make any enemy feel that it was a rather dangerous experiment to cross the border.
Puncture them.

Yes, puncture any enemy that would cross the border. We heard a great deal about the confidential scheme of the war office for the invasion of the Transvaal, but when the South African war broke out, there was not a solitary map of the Transvaal or Orange Free State in Britain. So far as the confidential report of the general is concerned, that has been discussed before, and I shall not reopen the discussion. I should be sorry to have anything said here which would tend to produce the slightest friction among tlie officers of the Militia Department. It has always been my aim and the aim of hon. members on this side to keep the issues in the Militia Department out of the arena of contentious discussion as much as possible, because we should all stand shoulder to shoulder in the upholding of our country. I have not had an opportunity of reading this famous report, but the hon. minister lias expressed himself in this House as very favourable to the views stated by the general. He has told us that he and the general are in a.ccord in all these matters. That being the case,
I am not disposed to probe too deep into any little wound or any confidential reports there may be in the department, but I trust that in due time these things will be used in the best interests of the militia. I may

inform the hon. minister that it is my intention, either on the militia estimates or on going into Committee of Supply, to take up the question of training the youth of the country in the use of the rifle. My whole aim is to get both young and old men trained in the use of firearms, so that should an enemy assail us, X care not whether our cousins to the south, or Invaders from any other quarter of the globe, they would hesitate before they crossed the Canadian border to face the lads of this country.

The MINISTER OFj MILITIA AND DEFENCE. I am afraid I cannot. Mr. FOWLER, I think that is a very proper thing. I would like to know the total enrolment in these associations.

speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to say that so far as high schools are concerned he did not provide this ammunition to them free. But I find an exception here, the Hamilton Collegiate Institute has been supplied with free ammunition. I think that all the institutes ought to be treated alike.

I suppose in that case they are connected with one of the corps, and are over 18 years of age. speechtext:
In regard to the Hamilton Collegiate Institute, I have the target returns in my possession for the senior corps. They are members of the regular rifle association and shoot over the long ranges. The junior corps shoot with the miniature ammunition. I do not know whether that ammunition has been supplied free or not. This is at 200, 500 and 600 yards for boys. Then they had one match of seven rounds rapid firing at 500 yards, and I find that the scores were very creditable. Out of a possible 35 one made 26, one made IS one made 17, 19, 15, 17, 11 and so on. The scores all through are very creditable. Although these are cadets in a collegiate institute, nevertheless they shoot with long range rifles, and at very long ranges. In the case of the junior cadets, they used miniature am-

munition and the score there for the boys ! from 12 to 14 years of age is remarkably creditable, and I will give it to the House later on.
Is it the intention of the minister to get authority to supply ammunition to the different schools throughout the country ?

We have it already, but we have not had enough ammunition to go round, so far. It is manufactured in Quebec. Next year, on account of the largely increased machinery, we expect to be able to manufacture over 2,000,000 rounds.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Is it a fact that to the * junior class in this collegiate institute at Hamiltion you have charged for the miniature ammunition supplied, or was it supplied free ?

speechtext: Is it the intention of the minister to get authority to supply the juniors ?

In the new Bill which has been prepared and of which notice has been given it is proposed to take that authority I stated the other night that I would be able to say whether I would bring down the Bill this session or not, but I am not prepared to say that to-night.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
It is a most inconsistent thing to supply the juniors with ammunition and make them pay for it, and to supply the seniors free. The reason cannot be that it is dangerous for the juniors, because it would be just as dangerous for the seniors. I am sorry to see the minister so indefinite in regard to introducing his Bill this session. Last session he gave us a promise that the Militia Act -would be amended so as to give these boys an opportunity of having free ammunition. There are several other things that should be provided in connection writh cadet corps. For instance, the arms are too heavy for them, as the hon. gentleman will see by his own report. More interest should be taken in the cadet corps. I hope the hon. gentleman will not overlook the importance of providing that these cadet corps should spend at least a short time in camp, perhaps for one day, subject to certain restrictions safeguarding and protecting Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).
them in such a way as that the parents of these small boys would not object to their attending camp. I trust the hon. gentleman will give this matter consideration.

I agree entirely with my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) and other hon. gentlemen who have indicated their opinion as to the importance of looking after tliesfe young cadets. At the same time it must not be forgotten that under our constitution the provinces have control of educational matters and this to a very large extent must come under their purview. I am making arrangements with some of the heads of the educational departments of the provinces with a view of trying to agree upon some plan by which we can do a little more to further the end which my hon. friends and myself have in view.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I would say that this is another point I purpose bringing up when this question is discussed at greater length, but now that we are on the question, and in view of the early coming on of the military camps, I will take the opportunity of giving the hon. minister a few suggestions and like the old medicine, if they will not do any good they will not do any harm. The target practice, even under the very capable instructors that are placed over these camps is largely, to use a mild term, wasted at the present time. The riflemen go down and practice at the targets. What the hon. Minister should see carried out is that every officer not only practices shooting, but that he also take hold of the squad and instruct the squad how to carry out its rifle practice. Then, when they get through with that they should go on to the long range and the officers and non-commissioned officers in turn should take charge of the instruction, because men learn by doing. It is all right for a man to stand off and see another giving directions, but unless lie gets into harness himself and has to put his men through the firing practice he is not as proficient as he otherwise would be. I have watched them frequently in camp. I watched them last year at the Niagara camp for part of a day. It was very nice-I will not say it was useless-but it was not as useful as it might have been. I just give the hon. minister these suggestions in order that if they commend themselves to him they may be carried out in the coming camps. I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has considered the proposition as to placing, not only rifles with all these Dominion associations and n couple of rifles in each school in the country for the use of the school associations, but ultimately of placing a rifle in the hands of every ablebodied man in the Dominion of Canada under proper auspices.

I would be delighted to do it, but

when I have only $35,000 for rifles. 1 And it very difficult.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I understood the hon. minister to say that a portion of this amount went in aid of military bands ?

The amount given to bands depends npou the number of men in the band and its efficiency. It ranges from $25 up to $100. It is given to all the bands throughout the country and to all the corps.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: In regard to the cadets, what is the limit of age ; that is, how old must they be before they can enter ?

Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Even at the risk of being somewhat unpopular, I have entertained the view for some time that there is a possibility of carrying this military spirit a little too far. There is no doubt whatever that we are fast developing by our system, or conduct, a strong military spirit all over the country and that we are attracting the youth of our country from the industrial pursuits of life. I notice that these military cadets are very popular in towns and villages. It is there you would expect them to be popular, but I notice as well that the youth of smaller towns and villages and those connected with country schools all over the country are taking it up very rapidly and there seems to be a strong and growing ambition to be connected with some military organization, military cadets, or military something. Many of them are showing the strong inclination owing to that to get away to the larger fields of life where they can be more intimately associated with military life than they are in the country villages or at the country schools. We have at present, in my judgment, too many attractions to draw the youth of the country away from the agricultural pursuits of life especially. This seems to be another one that may grow to dangerous proportions in future, and I am
merely throwing out this word of warning. While this is no doubt intended to be in the right direction there seems to be a possibility of starting an agitation that afterwards may grow beyond the proportions that we intended it should reach and beyond the proportions that are healthy in the interests of the country. I think we ought to be a little careful and not encourage it too much, because if it is continued and grows as rapidly in the future as it has in the past, it may be a trouble to this country, because we cannot keep it under control as we may desire to do. There is no question that this is one of the things to-day that is becoming very attractive to the youth of the country and is tending to draw very many away from home at an earlier period in life than perhaps they should be taken away in their own interests, or in the interest of their parents, or of the pursuits of life with which they are connected.

If there is no bard and fast rule by which the rifles of a battalion are to be kept entirely at the headquarters of the battalion, I would like to ask the consideration of the hon. minister to the request that the rifles of the two companies which have their headquarters at the town of Orillia may be kept there. In the cities it is much more easy to get up a feeling of kindliness, if I may so term it, towards the militia, owing to the fact that in cities the companies cultivate the social side of military life. In the town of Orillia one very attractive feature has been the friendly competition between the civilian corps of shooting men and those connected with the militia, but owing to the fact that the rifles are kept at the battalion headquarters at Barrie, these two companies have been without the attraction of rifle shooting that other companies have in the battalion. I would ask the hon. minister if these companies could have their rifles, and as the armoury is not as good there as might be desired, I would call his attention to the fact that in the public building used for the purposes of a post office and other government offices, there is a large room that I think is not in general use which might be used for the storage of these rifles.

I sympathize very much with the views expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett). I am very sorry indeed that a change was made in the rural battalions by making central! headquarters, and I am frank enough to admit that I think it was a mistake. There seemed to be some sort of extraordinary dread, when I came into office, in the mind of the then general officer commanding as to issuing the new rifle. The officers seemed to have an idea that it should be packed in cotton wool, and that the militiaman should be allowed to see it only once a year. We have outgrown that now. but the prevailing idea then was that we must not issue the rifles until there was

a central armoury and a competent armourer. In tlie meantime we liaye constructed certain armouries, and I suppose we feel under an obligation to make use of them ; but I think that the proposal made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) is perfectly fair, and I will take it into consideration and see whether his wishes in that regard cannot be carried into effect.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The theory to which the minister refers was due to the fact that the myth was abroad that once a rifle had been fired with cordite cartridge it must be cleaned immediately. I have a rifle that I have carried in 1S99 and 1900, and every year since, and it has not been cleaned once.
Oh, oh.

I may explain that it belongs to myself ; and though it never has been cleaned once, yet strange to say its bullet sometimes finds its billet. It has fired some thousands rounds of ammunition, and it is all right.
I think that is the general experience.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I am sorry the minister did not reply to the remarks of my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) in relation to the creation of a military spirit in the country. So far as I am concerned,
I would have every boy and, for that matter, every girl, in Canada imbued with the military spirit, and then you would never have to dread militarism. Our permanent ' corps are begging Canadians to join and they will not do so, but in a district where there is a proper military spirit abroad you will find our young men joining the volunteers enthusiastically.
The reason I did not reply to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) was because I felt that the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) could reply very much Jietter than I could.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Let me give an illustration of what I mean. Not very long ago I was passing a country school and saw a number of boys, ranging in years from nine to fourteen, each of them with a little wooden gun marching under the command of a small boy, and each with a cigarette in his mouth, puffing away for all he was worth.
Oh.
It did seem to me that the doctrine of teaching the young idea how to shoot had been inculcated into them too early in life, and that they had associated with it other habits of military life.

I have carried a gun for thirty-seven years, and I have never had a cigarette or a pipe in my mouth Sir F. W. BORDEN.
yet, so the two things do not go hand in hand.
Hear, hear.
There are few like my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes), and we cannot expect the ordinary individual to be the same as he is.

I disapprove of the idea that we should not encourage our boys to join the cadet corps. It is not so much that it creates a military spirit as that it promotes discipline and strength of character. If the member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) saw the cadet corps in connection with our Collegiate Institute, and saw those boys one day before they joined the cadets and two weeks afterwards, he would find them greatly improved.
Hear, hear.

The cadet corps creates discipline, it gives the boys a bearing which they preserve through life, and if they should ever be called to the defence of their country it imparts to them at all events the rudiments of military knowledge. I believe these cadet corps ought to be encouraged, and I believe the parents of our Canadian boys approve of them. The gentleman in St. Thomas who looks after the cadet corps there has received very great praise from the commanding officers for the discipline which he imparts to the boys. My hon. friend will find that could they have cadet corps in villages the same as we have in cities, and if he inquires into it, he will find that instead of encouraging the boys to smoke cigarettes it would train them to habits directly the opposite.
Hear, hear.

If it were confined to collegiate institutes the boys would have reached more mature years, and the system would not be so objectionable. My experience is that in nearly every rural school throughout the country the spirit is becoming so prevalent that children of seven or eight years are imbued with it.
Hear, hear.

Those acquainted with rural districts recognize that there are attractions in military life which draw the youth at too early an age from their quiet farm homes to the cities. We have been considering how we can prevent this depopulation of the agricultural districts. There are various reasons for it, and in my judgment this is one of them.

The argument of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) defeats itself. If the policy of having all the youth of the country trained in military exercises is carried out, there will be no need of these boys rushing to the cities and towns to indulge in military

training. I can say to him, with a good deal of pride-and the gallant and learned gentleman from Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) will endorse this statement-that at the time of the military review at Toronto, two years ago, some of the rural corps took second place to no corps from Toronto or any other city on that occasion.
Was that due to the system of military cadets inaugurated some years ago ?

To speak personally, I had the honour of leading a regiment which I think was considered second to none on that occasion, and I can assure the hon. member for East Grey that the efficiency of that regiment was largely due to the fact that many of the men had been trained in the schools before joining the volunteer corps. Fully one-half of one company and about one-third of another, were boys who had their training in the schools of the country previous to going into camp. The hon. member for East Elgin has very properly pointed out the great advantage of this training. Where do you find men with more respect for law and order than the old soldiers of this country ? You never find them indulging in disorder, except in an occasional celebration on pension day, and X am sure that my hon. friend from East Grey would not object to that. Where-ever you have a strong military spirit, you have more manhood in the youth of the country. As the hon. member for East Elgin says, when you have a boy who stands with his head erect and his' hands out of his pockets, you have the making of a man ; but when you see one standing with his head down and his hands in his pockets, and a streak of tobacco down his jaw, you can safely say that he is on the way to the gutter. I trust that the hon. member for East Grey will reconsider the conclusion he arrived at on seeing those boys going around with cigarettes in their mouths. I am surprised he did not stop them and read them a moral lecture. But I am sure that if he will make the school a present of a Union Jack and the teacher a present of a new bonnet for their proficiency in drill, the result will be that the boys will give up smoking.

X have no doubt the hon. member is able to give a great deal of valuable advice ; but I fail to see that he has advanced any logical reason why I should change my views on the subject. I admit that a military training does make boys look more manly ; that is in the right direction. But in many other directions I am afraid it is not for the well-being of the youth of the country. The hon. gentleman suggests that the member for East Grey might have read these boys a moral lecture. Well, he is perhaps not as much in the habit of reading moral lectures to 119
others as the hon. gentleman is, and there may be some excuse for my refraining.

I wish to point out that if the youth of the country are trained in the way we have been describing, the necessity will be avoided of the General Officer Commanding making such remarks as the following in his report:
For example, at Niagara-on-theLake this year, out of 1,054 non-commissioned officers there were not less than 440 who put on the stripes for the first time. Such a force certainly does not provide the trained frame-work needed to make a citizen army efficient in time of war.
As with seme of the non-commissioned officers, so it is with some of the officers.

speechtext: There has been a good deal of discussion throughout the press, especially in the old country, as to why Canada does not get on with her general officers commanding. If we are to judge by the verdict recorded by almost every one of these generals, each one found that his predecessor was absolutely useless. Discuss the matter with any imperial officer of high standing in the old land, and he will tell you that there are three types of generals sent out to this country. One of these was the second in command of a certain regiment, and in order to avoid having to give him the command of that famous regiment, he was shipped to Canada to get him out of the way. Another was sent but because they wanted to keep him a year or two longer on the full pay list. Another was such a born crank that they had no place for him in the service in the old country and so they sent him out to Canada. And another came out in order that he might make the Canadian militia a stepping stone to the position of commander in chief in the imperial service. For the first time in history, we have in Canada a general officer who was sent here by the imperial authorities on his superior merits. I have therefore no hesitation whatever in encouraging the House to increase his pay. I am thoroughly in favour of having an imperial trained officer to command our militia, but I am also thoroughly in favour of reforming the training of the imperial officer. The fact that in many cases these officers have been failures in Canada is not necessarily due to any fault on the part of the people in Canada, but because the pay was not sufficient to attract an officer considered fit to take the position, and inferior men were sent out. This is what you will be told by officers high in the imperial service in the old country. But we have to-day a general officer commanding who is a credit to the imperial service, who is an ornament to the British empire, whether you take him as a gentleman or a soldier, and I should be very glad to see his salary increased to what it should be. If such were done, we could look forward to having the proper men sent out to command our militia.

Since my hon. friend has been in charge of the Militia Department, the pay of the general officer commanding has been raised to a figure which we thought would be an inducement to officers, such as the one we have now, to take the position. As to our former generals, I do not think that the gossip which my hon. friend heard in England is at all applicable to them, nor do I think it desirable to repeat gossip of that kind reflecting on gentlemen who are no longer at the head of our militia, but who served us well when in this country. When we discussed the question of pay, we compared the amount these officers get in the other colonies and

increased ours accordingly, and I apprehend that the gentleman who is here now understood what pay he was going to get when he accepted the post, and that pay compares fairly with what is paid by the other colonies.

I owe no apology to this House or anybody else for the comments I have made. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that he was not long enough Minister of Militia to know very much about it. Take these generals, and the fact that they have all run foul against the various Canadian governments has reflected adversely on this country in more ways than one. I know that that subject has been discussed in the old country very recently, and the fact that there has been occasion for such discussion is due to no fault on the part of the Canadian people or government. This remark is applicable to past governments as well as to the present one. As regards the increases of salary, I was the first to bring that matter up and I fought it to a finish. I found that the little colony of New South Wales was giving its officer commanding a higher salary than this Dominion was giving, with its population of 5,000,000 and its immense resources. To-day we should still further increase the salary of the general officer commanding. I maintain that we can very properly increase the pay to what it should be and encourage not only this officer to remain but similar officers to come to this country.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria), takes the responsibility of saying these things for himself, of course, he bears his responsibility. But what I understood him as stating before was the gossip he heard in England. If he speaks of his own experience and sentiments, I have nothing to say about it. But, I will say that the gentlemen who have come here from England have been, as a rule, capable men, and they have served this country well by helping materially to bring our militia force to the splendid state in which it now is. And I may repeat that it will not help the position of this country, nor will it improve the opinion held of Canada in the old country, to bring these things up with regard to gentlemen who have served us for some time and have returned to their regiments and to take the rank they were entitled to at home.

As one who is not a military man, I may be permitted to state, how, in my opinion, this strikes a good many people throughout the country. To many it is inexplicable that nearly every general officer commanding who comes out is praised very highly for a time after he comes, leaving us to think that we have the best officer commanding that could be secured. but, after a time, there is dissatisfaction and grumbling, and these keep increasing until it must be very unpleasant

for the general officer commanding if he tries to remain throughout the natural length of his term of office. I think the impression is that we have had some good general officers, notwithstanding that dissatisfaction has been expressed before they left the country. The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) said-I forget whether he intimated that it was a remark he heard on the other side of the water-that the general officers came in contact with snags over here. In defence of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, who might otherwise be thought to be one of the ' snags ' I think I might ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) to whom he intended to refer by that expression.
Certainly not to the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) who I regret to say, has been very sycophantic to some of the gentlemen.

Perhaps I may be expected at this point to say a single word. There is a great deal of truth in what the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) says as to the salary given to the general officer commanding. It is, no doubt, true that Canada pays less than any other colony of the British Empire to an officer of equal rank. I do not think however, that that fact makes very much difference in the class of officers
speakername: The MINISTER OP MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Yes, it does.

Well, I think the fact that Canada occupies a leading position among the colonies of the British Empire makes the position here sought after, and officers are rather anxious to get here. For instance, I happen to know of a gentleman who was offered a position of very much higher emolument, but declined it in order to come here. That is some proof of the correctness of my argument. That, however, is not a very good argument as bearing upon the question, whether we are paying our general officer commanding adequately or not. I think that that is a very good subject for consideration. On that point I can only refer to what I said the other night. I do do not care to be drawn into that discussion again, except, perhaps, to repeat one observation I made the other day, and that is that while gentlemen who have been sent out here have been very good soldiers, they have not been men with the kind of experience necessary to qualify them to occupy the very delicate and difficult position which the general officer commanding occupies in this self-governing country at the head of the militia force. Most of these gentlemen- all of them in fact-are regular soldiers accustomed to command in the regular army and men who have not had experience in the war office in connection with the executive of the mother country or any other country. I will not add anything more.

Would the hon. gentleman tell us what the department has to do with the cartage of goods ?

There is an examination required, under the Act, of one case of merchandise out of every ten. If there are only two cases, one of them must go to the examining warehouse for examination. The department pays for the cartage of those goods thus taken to the examining warehouse, and as there is a large increase in the importation of goods, the cartage account has also increased.
