All these are temporary employees. Is there any way of avoiding that and of placing these employees on the permanent list ?

At Montreal-I have not the figures under my hand now, but I dare say there are a hundred temporary employees. Perhaps I should not say that, but there are over fifty and running up to one hundred, who are what are known as temporary employees. These are men who have not passed the civil service examination and have not been placed upon the permanent list by Order in Council. Many of them, while they are called temporary, necessarily owing to the distinction which the Act makes, are really as permanent in one sense as any of the other officers who have been placed on the permanent list. I would be very glad to place them on it also. They have urged it upon me and put pressure upon me to get on
for the very obvious reason that a temporary officer under the law, as it is now, if he is taken sick, cannot receive his pay. He is not entitled to his three weeks' leave of absence, and, therefore, the temporary employees are very anxious to get on the permanent list. I have told them that if they will only pass the qualifying examination, which is requisite for that purpose under the Act, I will be only too pleased to put them on, because, as it is, it works a hardship upon these men. There are some men who have been twelve or fifteen years in the service and who are just as good and just as faithful officers as others who are on the permanent list. We have a number of men who come on in the summer and we let them go in the winter. But, I am speaking of a number of men who have been in the service for ten or twelve years or more, who are on the temporary list, and who would like to get on the permanent list. I say to them : I would be only too pleased to put you on if you pass your qualifying examination. I dare say that when they left school they could have passed the qualifying examination such ns is prescribed under the Civil Service Act, but they are afraid to try it now and do not do it. But, there is only one office to which we can appoint them without passing the examination that is to the position of preventive officer. A collector at a port does not have to pass the examination. The appraiser at a port does not necessarily have to pass the civil service qualifying examination, but he has to pass a special examination, the reason for which hon. gentlemen will see as he has to be an expert as to the quality and value of goods. In many cases I have appointed some of these men who have been faithful officers to positions as preventive officers. The office has no particular, designated duties. We appoint them and assign them to this position or that position. But as long as the Act remains as it is, requiring that these officers should pass the civil service examination, I hesitate to place them on the permanent list in a general way, but I am trying to induce them to pass the examination. There are men who have been in the service a long time and who can do their duty as well as younger men who can pass this examination, and in regard to these I have felt warranted in appointing a good many of them to the position of preventive officer, although a good many of them have not been appointed in that way yet. They are virtually permanent men as far as remaining in the service is concerned. The greater bulk of them were employed before I was charged with the department, and they have remained on. One result of the disability they are under is that if they get sick, the collector must certify that they have worked so many days and he can only certify to the number of days that a man has worked and unless he'gets such a certificate the wages are not

paid. This is a hardship on these men. Formerly, wheh the old Superannuation Act was in force, it was a matter of greater consequence than it is at present not to be on the permanent list, because, when an officer on the permanent list became aged, he retired upon the superannuation fund. Of course that does not come in now, because, with the new law, there is a certain amount retained from the salaries of the permanent employees which the government give to them with interest compound when they leave the service, but there still remains the difficulty that if they have lost time through illness they are not entitled to their wages as the permanent employee is with whom they are working side by side.

The reasons given by the minister are very good for not putting them on the permanent list, but the strange thing is that we constantly see civil servants appointed who have not passed the examination. To-night we were told that Martineau had not passed the examination, but he started on a salary of $700 a year.
That is the inside service.
What is the difference between the inside service and the outside service, when the Act provides that both must pass the qualifying examination ?

It can be said for the members of the outside service that many of them have passed the age when they could go up for the civil service examination. I know personally that there are many men in the outside service who are just as capable, and perhaps more capable. than those who have passed the examination in the inside service. In the case of bonded goods leaving a ship these officers are there to deliver them, and they must keep a correct memorandum of their work, and sometimes they are employed at night as well as at day. I have had some experience, and I know from personal observation that there are men who are engaged in that service who are most capable men, and as a rule they are very much underpaid.

Has the minister come to any conclusion as to a change in the system by which the transportation companies now pay some of our customs officers for night work and overtime ? The present system, as explained to me, does not seem to be very satisfactory. I understand that objections to it have been presented to the hon. gentleman, and I would like to know whether he thinks there is any good ground for these objections.

I will have to bring in a supplementary estimate to provide for that service for 1903-4. I am not unmindful of the request made a year ago by the hon. gentleman that we should Hon. Mr. PATERSQN.
estimate our expenditure more closely, and I think it is very desirable that we should when possible, and it certainly would be more convenient and more pleasant, if we did not have to ask for a supplementary estimate. The fact, however, is that the business has increased so rapidly that we have hesitated each year, and this session I will have to ask for a supplementary estimate of something like $100,000 for the purpose of paying these amounts to officers to which the leader of the opposition refers. It arises in this way : The hours for officers in the outside service are from eight o'clock in the morning to six in the evening. At all the frontier ports you must have men on duty at night to meet trains or boats, and up to the present the pay of these officers has been charged to the transportation companies. It was said to my predecessors in office, and it has been said to myself : It is the duty of the government to give every facility to trade and commerce, and as it would not be reasonable that you should ask that trains should be run between eight in the morning and six at night, you should pay your own officers for being on duty when we do run our trains. Hitherto we have said to the companies : You may run your trains and we will put our officers there, but it is for your convenience and you must pay for them. Their argument was : You recognize that it is your duty to give every facility to trade and commerce, and your officers are there to guard the revenue of the Dominion, and it is the duty of the Dominion to pay their salaries ; if you have to have your officers there at night as [DOT] well as in day time, you should pay them for their services instead of making us pay.
I have never been able to answer their argument to my own satisfaction, and I feel now that it is only just that we should accede to their wishes. I have always felt that it was anomalous that our Dominion officers should receive pay from transportation companies.
Hear, hear.

The transportation companies pay this amount to the collector and the collector pays it out to the men who have earned it, so that the officers were not paid direct by the companies. I will have to ask for $100,000 in the supplementary estimates, but we may be able to economize, so that perhaps we shall not require to use the whole of it. Hon. gentlemen know from the conservative and prudent manner in which that department is managed that the money will not be spent if not needed. Occasionally an officer will be required by the transportation companies purely for their own convenience, and we will still make them pay in that case. For example, the Grand Trunk Railway in competition with other companies will find it to their convenience to have a Canadian officer at Boston say, who will forward goods through in bond. That offi-

speechtext: I asked the hon. gentleman for a comparison of the total cost of the Customs Department in 1895-6, and in 1901-2. As he did not give it, I will give the figures, having before me the estimates of 1895-6. For this same service for which we are now asked to vote $1,059,000, the estimates for 1895-6 were $801,580, an increase of $258,000 by the hon. gentleman since he came in to administer what he calls this economical department. Taking all the expenses together, for which he asks $1,301,505, the same work was done in 1895-6 for $874,285, an increase of $427,000, or nearly half a million-over fifty per cent of an increase. It is true, the imports have increased, the business of the offices has increased somewhat, and more money has been collected; but because more money has been collected, it does not necessarily mean that there should be half a million dollars paid to extra officers to collect it. At the port of Ganan-oque. where the business has probably doubled, the same officer has done the work during the past year who did it in 1895-6. There has been no increase there, and why should there be an increase in other ports ? Because a man who imported $100 worth in 1895-6, imports $1,000 worth now, there is no more work in making the entry or taking the money. My hon. friend speaks of percentages. That is a nice way of putting it. He says he collected more money at a smaller percentage of cost than his predecessor; but that is not a fair comparison, in regard to running the Department of Customs. The bare fact is there, that the hon. gentleman has increased the expenditure of his department nearly half a million dollars, and then he says it is an economically managed department.

I think the hon. gentleman's remarks will not commend themselves to the fairness of the committee. Does he actually think it possible to do double the amount of business on the same expenditure as before ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I think it possible in the hon. gentleman's business, or any other business in the country. Many merchants and manufacturers have doubled their business, but have not increased their staff or their expenses twenty-five or even ten per cent. . The hon. gentleman knows that his own business has probably increased to two or three times what it was in 1895-6, but his expenses have not increased accordingly. No manufacturing concern in the country wotfld sustain the hon. gentleman in increasing his expenditure practically fifty per cent over what it was under the late administration, in order to collect a little more revenue.

I have not myself been in business lately, but when I was we were doing a continually increasing business, and we found that our expenses were continually increasing, in doing it. The hon. gentleman's experience may not be the same. He has quoted the expenses of the year 1895-6; but that is not a fair comparison, because when I assumed office the estimates for the year were not sufficient; part of the expenses of that year had to be paid in the following year. But we will take the year before that, 1894-5, which was a complete year under the late controller, who I think was considered to manage the department very well. How much did it cost in that year to collect the revenues of this country ? As I said, you cannot collect $35,000,000 of revenue, which represents so many more goods arriving in the country, so many more packages to be examined and carted, so many more entries to be made, so many more clerks to be employed to do the work, at the same cost as half the amount. You must apply the rule of percentages. In 1894-5 the cost of collection was $5.13 for every $100 collected ; in 1901-2, the cost was $3.62. If we apply the rate of cost of collection of 1894-5 to the revenue of 1901-2, I would have paid $1,663,429 to collect last year's revenue. In other words, if the percentage of cost of collection last year had been the same as it was in 1894-5, I would have spent $487,405 more than I did. That is the amount of the saving. The hon. gentleman says, you do not expect the same proportion of increase in expenditure. No, we do not, but we do expect an increase. We expect this year, if the revenue keeps up, that it will be collected at a less rate than it has been collected in the country before. Any business man must know that when the revenue is doubled, there is more work to be done at the custom-houses. The habit of trade now is, with the facilities which we have for transportation, that people, instead of buying in such large quantities as they did before, do very much more in the way of repeat orders. They make smaller purchases more often renewed. That means more work and more entries. I grant that

if a clerk is working at a desk and has an entry of $1,000, if it is a short invoice, he can perhaps attend to it just as quickly as he could attend to a $100 invoice containing the same number of items. But for the extra work that requires to he done, extra men must be employed. I have not mentioned the extra ports that have been opened, I have not spoken of the increase of business in all parts of the Dominion, or of our desire to give some of our officers higher salaries, who are not paid sufficiently for the work they do. This will be part of the increase we ask, but we are keeping in mind the reduction of the percentage of the cost of collection. If we can keep that reduced to the extent we have been doing, fair minded business men will admit that the department must be fairly well managed. There is no use in saying that we can collect $35,000,000 with the same expense as $17,000,000. We cannot have the imports of the country nearly doubled without putting increased work on the appraisers staff and the clerical staff, and your landing waiters. Then there is the opening of new ports. I have now about twenty applications for new ports in places that where they say trade has so increased that new ports are required. I cannot give all the new ports demanded, but I do what I can. I can assure you that our officers are earning their salaries and that a good many of them are not paid what they should be, considering the present conditions, and while we may not be able to meet the views of all of them, we think that there are certain cases so strong that we must make an effort to do them justice.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman talks about the increased work causing increased expenditure. Let him take the port of Gan-anoque and he will find that although the business there has doubled, and although the amount collected has trebled, the expenses have not increased, and the staff is the same. Why should not the same result be found at Montreal and other ports ? The hon. gentleman does not want to compare the year 1895-96 with the present, but wants to go back to 1894-5, when the depression was still greater, in order to make a comparison of percentages. Well, let him take 1896-7, when he had complete control, and when he asked for a vote to pay the deficiency of the late government. With the same items that he is asking for to-day, he had the work done for $956,000 for which he is now asking $1,300,000.
What was the revenue last year ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
That has nothing to do with it. Take the port of Gananoque, the revenue increased there, but not the expense. The fact is that at Ottawa and at Montreal and at other places, the department is overrun with labour not required, and in order to make places for hungry Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
heelers, since 1896-7 the hon. gentleman has increased the expenditure of his department $345,000.
It will be $100,000 next year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We will not find fault with that, because it is taken off the transportation companies and put on the government ; but compared with 1896-7, the hon. gentleman is asking $345,000 more for the same work and the same staff, though, of course, some more taxes have been collected and more burdens have been put upon the people. The hon. gentleman compares percentages, but it costs no more to collect $1,000 than $100. In none of the departments are the officers overworked. I know the customs work that has to be done at my out port, and I know that the employees there do not do the work that is done in factories or in business offices or anything like it.

There are many ports where the salaries have not been advanced, owing to the fact that the officials formerly had not much to do, and could easily do a good deal more work, and Gananoque may be one of these. But where the business of ports has increased as it has done in Montreal, it must be evident that the expenditure has to be increased. It is impossible to do $1,000,000 more business without increasing the expenditure. Why, the receipts at Winnipeg, when I took office, were about half a million. They are nearly $2,000,000. It is simply impossible to have that extra work done without increasing the expenditure. Of course, we could let the work go, we could give the people their goods, but it is our bounden duty to have sufficient officers to collect the revenue. Where you have the cost of collection reduced from $5 per $100 to $3.50, that shows that the expenditure is not increasing in ratio to the increase of business. The proper test is the number of entries and the actual clerical work which is performed. If $35,000,000 worth of goods come to this country there must be nearly the double number of packages that came in when only $17,000,000 worth of goods were entered. These packages have to be opened and examined and attended to by the landing waiters. They have to be checked and entered by the clerks in the long room, and all the different branches of the department must necessarily have more work thrust upon them. Then in addition you have ports, such as Depot Harbour, where no revenue is collected, but where you must have two and perhaps three men to attend to the transshipment of grain. We must have men at Coteau when grain is going through. You have to have this, though it adds to your expenditure and does not show any revenue at all. I maintain that the department is worked as economically as it is possible to work it, to safeguard the re-

venue and collect what ought properly to be collected. If I were to be pressed further in that direction, and some hon. gentleman were to ask me :	Are you sure you have
enough officers at certain ports to efficiently safeguard the revenue ? I do not know that I should he able to give as satisfactory an answer as I am to the question whether we employ too many of them. Do not let hon. gentlemen judge the whole service by a port like Gananoque, where at one time the officers had not enough to do to occupy their time, and where more work could easily be done without increased expenditure. The increase in such a port has not the same effect upon the expenditure as the increase in Montreal, Winnipeg and other large ports throughout the country.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) to say that the per capita cost of collecting the customs had decreased or merely the percentage on the amount collected ?
The percentage.

Then he does not contend that the per capita cost has decreased ?
The! MINISTER OF CUSTOMS. You do not judge it by the per capita cost ?

I think the hon. gentleman, in the criticisms he made of the Customs Department some years ago when he was on this side, used as one of his arguments figures intended to show that the per capita cost had increased. Of course, if his experience has caused him to repent, he has improved to that extent since 1890.
I never based it on the per capita cost.
I think the hon. gentleman used that argument in his criticisms in this House.
Oh, no. If I did, I know better now.
The hon. gentleman has learned something
1 do not admit that I needed to learn, and I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) could prove it.
Perhaps hon. gentlemen will like a little further time to consider these items.

I think we have made substantial progress, for the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Paterson) has been enabled to take about two-thirds of the time in explaining matters to us at enormous length. I admit they require explanation, but I do not think that this side have had a fair chance at the item yet. Therefore, perhaps, the hon. Postmaster General would permit the committee to rise at this stage ?
And not take an item at all ?

The hon. gentleman has had two-thirds or three-quarters of this item, so far as the time necessary for its discussion is concerned. The progress has been ample, I think. It is a very comprehensive item as I think the hon. gentleman will see.
That is why I want it to go through.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will bring down the figures with regard to Gananoque in 1896 and 1903. Meantime I would point out to him that the other institutions of the country, such as the banking institutions, are doing double the business they did in 1896 and yet their expenses have not increased. There is hardly a bank but is doing double or treble the business it did before handling more cash, receiving and discounting more notes, yet with practically no increase in expenses.
Somebody was asking where Gananoque was.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman gets the figures from the customs he will learn.
It was intimated here that, probably in 1896, there were twice too many employees in the Gananoque office and that is why the number has never been increased since.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It has always been run by one man.

Well, it could hardly have been run by less.
Some resolutions reported.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock) moved the adjournment of the House.
What business is to be taken up on Monday ?

Part of the private member's business for Monday remains, and private Bills and questions. Then there are the two Bills in the hands of private members which, I believe, have been fixed for Monday-Bills relating to the Fruit Marks Act, in the hands of the hon. member for Ilalton (Mr. Henderson) and the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith). After these are disposed of, we shall proceed with government business, proceeding first, I think with the Railway Commission Bill, though I have not been able to see my colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals on that subject. After that, I think we shall take up Supply, proceeding probably with the estimates of the Minister of Customs or the Minister of Railways and

Canals. I do not know whether there are any government Bills to be proceeded with but X would like to have it understood that, if there are any, the government will be privileged to move them.
Mr. BOItDEN (Halifax). I think it would be advisable, in order to expedite the business of the House, that we should have as distinct a statement as possible at adjournment of the work at the next sitting, otherwise it is not always convenient for us to arrange that the gentlemen on this side more particularly interested in the different branches of the House shall be present and ready to proceed at the proper time.
The TOSTMASTER GENERAL,. I think that what I have outlined will pretty well exhaust the day-first there is the private members' business, then the Railway Commission Bill, followed by Supply, taking up the estimates of the Customs Department. I should think, considering the progress made this evening, that, perhaps, these items alone will be a ' piece de resistance ' for Monday. If not, we will proceed with the railway estimates.

What I understand from my hon. friend the Postmaster General is that we may expect, so far as the government business is concerned, the Railway Commission Bill, after that the estimates of the Minister of Customs, and after that, if any other business is taken up, it will be the estimates of the Minister of Railways and Canals.

My hon. friend the Minister of Customs thinks that perhaps the Minister of Railways and Canals may be occupied a part of the evening with a conference over his Railway Commission Bill outside of the House. If so, we will [DOT] proceed with the estimates of the Department of the Interior instead. But as the Minister of Railways and Canals has commenced his estimates it would be advisable to continue them. But, there will be the estimates of the Department of Customs.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.35 p.m.
Monday, June 1, 1903.
